savedReports.content: Question 1 In the State of O'Quinn, a defendant has committed the tort of "conversion" if (a) the plaintiff has rightful possession of a piece of property, (b) the defendant intentionally takes that property, and (c) the defendant did not have permission to take the property. P sues D for conversion. Assume that the case is in federal court. And assume that the following is the relevant text of P's Complaint: P had a car, which P bought last year. D drove off with P's car. While driving off, D shouted, "Haha, I took your car!" D did not ask for, nor did P give, P's permission to take the car. P therefore requests $100,000 in damages for the fair market value of the car. D files a motion to dismiss, arguing that the Complaint has failed to cite the O'Quinn state statutes and caselaw establishing the tort of conversion. You are the judge in the case: Is D right that the Complaint should be dismissed on this basis? (Remember, although it's state tort law, we're in federal court for this hypo, so the federal standard we learned applies. We'll learn when a state-law case can be in federal court later this semester.) Answer: No, D is wrong and the Complaint should not be dismissed on this basis. Explanation: Federal notice pleading under Rule 8(a)(2), as construed by Twombly/Iqbal, requires only "a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief" — i.e., factual allegations sufficient to make the claim plausible. A complaint never needs to cite the statutes or case law establishing the elements of a claim; that is a legal-research task for briefing, not a pleading requirement. Here P's factual allegations (rightful possession, intentional taking, lack of permission) map directly onto every element of conversion and plausibly entitle P to relief, so dismissal is unwarranted. Question 2 If a lawyer who is planning to bring a case in federal court is worried that their Complaint does not allege sufficient facts to make it "plausible," they can: Answer: (E) Both A and C. Explanation: A lawyer may always do more factual investigation (A) — asking the client follow-up questions and researching further. A lawyer may also plead facts on information and belief (C) where the facts are plausible and the lawyer has a reasonable basis to think evidentiary support will emerge after discovery, which courts (applying Twombly/Iqbal) permit especially where facts are not yet fully accessible to the pleader. Inventing facts (B) is never permissible — it would violate Rule 11(b)'s requirement that factual contentions have (or will likely have) evidentiary support, so any option including B (B alone, or "Both A and B") is wrong. Question 3 In Swanson v. Citibank, the court writes that "the plaintiff must give enough details about the subject-matter of the case to present a story that holds together." True or false: that means that the Complaint must tell a story that does not contradict itself. Answer: False. Explanation: A "story that holds together" is Judge Posner's shorthand for plausibility, not merely internal consistency. A complaint could be entirely free of self-contradiction and still fail Twombly/Iqbal if the alleged facts don't add up to a plausible entitlement to relief (e.g., they're too conclusory, too sparse, or describe a scenario that, while not self-contradictory, isn't a believable account of unlawful conduct). "Holding together" demands a coherent, plausible narrative supported by sufficient factual detail — a higher bar than simple non-contradiction. Question 4 P sues D. P requests that D waive service, per Rule 4(d). D waives service. The next thing that D does is file an Answer, 80 days after receiving the request to waive service. Is the Answer timely? Answer: No. Explanation: Under Rule 4(d)(3), a defendant who timely waives service has 60 days from the date the waiver request was sent to answer (90 days if the defendant was outside any U.S. judicial district). Filing 80 days after receiving the request exceeds that 60-day window, so the Answer is untimely. Question 5 P sues D. You are the attorney for D. After receiving P's Complaint, you draft and file D's Answer. Fifty days later, you realize that there was likely insufficient service of process, per Rule 12(b)(5). But that argument was not included in your Answer. Can you raise it now? Answer: No. Explanation: Insufficient service of process under Rule 12(b)(5) is one of the "disfavored" defenses (along with lack of personal jurisdiction, improper venue, and insufficient process) that Rule 12(h)(1) deems waived if not raised in a pre-answer Rule 12 motion or included in the answer itself. Because the Answer was already filed without this defense, and 50 days have passed (well beyond the 21-day window in which Rule 15(a)(1)(B) would allow amending the Answer as a matter of course), the defense is waived and cannot be raised now. Question 6 P sues D. You are the attorney for D. After receiving P's Complaint, you draft and file D's Answer. Fifty days later, you realize that there is likely no subject-matter jurisdiction, per Rule 12(b)(1). But that argument was not included in your Answer. Can you raise it now? Answer: Yes. Explanation: Subject-matter jurisdiction is never waived. Rule 12(h)(3) provides that a court must dismiss the action whenever it determines subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking, and this defense can be raised by any party (or the court itself) at any stage of the litigation, even after judgment. This is unlike the disfavored defenses in Question 5, which are waived if not timely raised. Question 7 P sues D. You are the attorney for D. You make a timely Rule 12(b)(5) motion for insufficient service of process, on the ground that you never got a copy of the Complaint. You win your motion, and P provides a copy of the Complaint. The next day, you read the Complaint. You think it doesn't meet the "plausibility" standard. So you would like to make a 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim. Can you do so? Answer: No. Explanation: Rule 12(g)(2)'s consolidation rule bars a party who has already made one Rule 12 motion from making a second Rule 12 motion raising a defense that was available but omitted from the first motion. Having already filed a 12(b)(5) motion, D cannot now file a separate 12(b)(6) motion. This differs from Question 5's waiver, though: failure to state a claim is one of the defenses Rule 12(h)(2) specially preserves, so it isn't lost entirely — D can still raise it in the Answer, in a Rule 12(c) motion for judgment on the pleadings after the pleadings close, or at trial. What's unavailable is bringing it as a fresh, standalone pre-answer Rule 12(b) motion.

# Exercise 8.1.1: Identifying When Terms in a Statute Apply to Your Client's Facts

**Question:** Underline, circle, or highlight the words of the statute that may be applicable to Bitters's potential case so that you can provide an initial response.

**Statute (N.Y. Civ. Rights Law § 51):**

"Any person whose **name, portrait, picture** or voice is used **within this state** **for advertising purposes** or for the purpose of trade **without having obtained the written consent of such person**, or if a minor of his or her parent or guardian, may maintain an equitable action . . . to prevent and restrain the use thereof, and may also sue and recover damages for any injuries sustained by reason of such use."

(Bolded/marked terms above are the ones that apply to Bitters's facts.)

**Answer — term-by-term application:**

- **"Any person"** — Bitters is a natural person, so this threshold requirement is satisfied.
- **"picture"** — The statute protects a person's "name, portrait, picture or voice." Sunblock, Inc. used a *photograph* of Bitters, which is squarely a "picture." Note the statute is written in the disjunctive (name, portrait, picture, *or* voice), so Bitters does not need his name or voice to have been used — the picture alone is enough. ("name" and "voice" are not applicable on these facts, since only his image was used, not his name or voice; "portrait" likely does not apply distinctly from "picture" but the statute doesn't require both.)
- **"is used within this state"** — Bitters was photographed on a rooftop in upstate New York, and nothing suggests the ad ran outside New York; this element appears satisfied, though counsel would want to confirm where the advertisement was actually published/displayed.
- **"for advertising purposes"** — The photo appeared in an advertisement for Sunblock, Inc.'s suntan products, with the tagline "Smear it, Don't burn it." This is a direct, commercial advertising use, satisfying this element clearly (the "purpose of trade" language is a separate, broader alternative that likely isn't even needed here since "advertising purposes" is so plainly met).
- **"without having obtained the written consent of such person"** — Bitters was asleep with a towel over his face when photographed and only saw the photographer as he was leaving; nothing in the facts indicates he consented, written or otherwise. This element appears satisfied.
- **"or if a minor of his or her parent or guardian"** — Not applicable; nothing indicates Bitters is a minor.
- **"may maintain an equitable action . . . to prevent and restrain the use thereof"** and **"may also sue and recover damages for any injuries sustained by reason of such use"** — These identify the two remedies available if the above elements are met: an injunction against further use of the photo, and money damages for injuries caused by the use.

**Initial response to the client:** Based on the phone notes, Bitters appears to have a viable claim under § 51 — his "picture" was used "for advertising purposes" within New York, without his written consent. The facts that would need further confirmation are (1) exactly where/how widely the ad was published, and (2) whether any consent was obtained through some other means not mentioned in the call notes.

---

# Exercise 8.2.1: Evaluating Excerpts of Application Sections for Effectiveness

**Governing rule/case illustration:** An owner owes a duty to assist an invitee if the invitee is helpless *and* the owner places the invitee in danger. *Osterlind v. Hill*, 160 N.E. 301, 302 (Mass. 1928). In *Osterlind*, the intoxicated invitee clung to an overturned canoe for half an hour, yelling for help, while the defendant listened but did nothing; the court held there was no duty because the invitee's own extended self-rescue efforts showed he was capable of exercising care for himself — i.e., he was not "helpless."

**Question 1:** "Rich's case is distinguishable from the facts in Osterlind. In Osterlind, the invitee caused his own imperilment and acted to protect himself by calling for assistance, which the court viewed as an indication that the invitee was not helpless. Such was not the case here. Thus, Rich likely has a claim against the Nighty-Night Motel." Effective or not effective?

**Answer: Not effective.** The excerpt correctly states the *Osterlind* rule but then fails to apply it. "Such was not the case here" is a bare conclusion — it never identifies *which* Rich facts show he did not (or could not) protect himself the way Osterlind did. Good application requires specific facts placed side-by-side with the case facts (e.g., how long Rich could function on his own, whether he called for help and for how long, what happened after he asked Gerald for help). Without that factual analogy, the reader has no way to evaluate whether the distinction actually holds, and the conclusion ("Rich likely has a claim") is unsupported.

**Question 2:** "Like in Osterlind, where Hill did not provide help to Osterlind, Gerald, the pool attendant, made Rich leave the pool without medical attention and told him to 'sleep it off,' even though Rich was dizzy and disoriented." Effective or not effective?

**Answer: Not effective.** This excerpt states a factual similarity (both defendants failed to render aid) but never connects that similarity to the *legal standard* — helplessness. In *Osterlind*, the failure to help did *not* create liability, precisely because the victim wasn't helpless. By analogizing only the "no help given" conduct without addressing the helplessness element, this excerpt actually risks proving too little (or cutting against Rich, since the same "no help" fact pattern produced no duty in *Osterlind*). Effective application needs to explain *why* the failure to help matters here — i.e., that it satisfies the second prong (placing an already-helpless invitee in danger) rather than standing alone.

**Question 3:** "Ignoring Rich's dizziness, Gerald offered Rich substandard advice to 'sleep off' a head injury. Gerald's offer of advice differs from the facts in Osterlind, where Hill did not provide assistance to Osterlind. Rich will argue that a reasonable person could foresee that he was walking unsteadily, thus helpless. Rich was in danger of passing out and therefore in no condition to walk home unaided." Effective or not effective?

**Answer: Not effective.** The characterization of the facts is internally inconsistent and therefore misleading. Telling an injured guest to "sleep it off" and sending him away is not meaningfully different from Hill's silence in *Osterlind* — both are failures to render real assistance to someone in trouble. Framing "sleep it off" as differing from "did not provide assistance" mischaracterizes the analogy and weakens credibility. In addition, the sentence "Rich will argue that a reasonable person could foresee... thus helpless" conflates foreseeability (a negligence/duty concept) with the "helpless" factual standard from *Osterlind* without explaining the connection, making the reasoning muddled rather than clear.

**Question 4:** "Unlike the invitee in Osterlind, Rich was verbally recognized by the pool attendant to be intoxicated and was asked to leave the pool area. Rich did not heed the request, but this distinction is not controlling." Effective or not effective?

**Answer: Not effective.** This excerpt identifies a real factual distinction (Gerald recognized/verbalized that Rich seemed intoxicated and told him to leave) but then dismisses it in a single conclusory clause — "this distinction is not controlling" — without any reasoning. An effective application section must explain *why* a raised distinction doesn't matter (e.g., because the relevant legal question is whether Rich was helpless *after* hitting his head and asking for help, not whether he was initially told to leave the pool). Simply asserting the conclusion invites the reader to disagree without any way to test the claim.

**Question 5:** "Rich will likely be able to prove that he was helpless, and that Gerald had a duty to provide medical aid. Immediately after Rich hit his head, he could barely lift himself out of the pool, was disoriented from the injury, and asked Gerald for help. Unlike the Osterlind victim, who was able to hang on for thirty minutes, Rich needed help right away. In Osterlind, the court held that the victim was not helpless because he was able to hang onto a canoe for thirty minutes. In the present case, the action was much more immediate; Rich fell shortly after leaving the pool. Gerald, the pool attendant, failed to recognize Rich's helplessness and then put him in a situation of peril by making him leave immediately without medical attention when Rich was dizzy and disoriented." Effective or not effective?

**Answer: Effective.** This is the strongest excerpt because it does what the others fail to do: it states a clear conclusion, then walks through *both* elements of the rule with specific, comparable facts. It draws a precise factual contrast with *Osterlind* (thirty minutes of self-sustained effort versus Rich's immediate collapse) tied directly to the "helpless" standard, explains *why* that distinction matters (immediacy of need versus demonstrated capacity for self-care), and separately addresses the "placed in danger" prong (Gerald made Rich leave without medical attention while dizzy and disoriented). Because every factual point is explicitly linked back to an element of the governing rule, the reasoning is transparent and persuasive rather than conclusory.

## Exercise 7.1.5: Crafting a Rule from a Series of Cases

**Note on missing material:** The attached exercise document includes only one of the four case summaries referenced ("read the following four case summaries") — *Goddard v. Boston & M. R. R. Co.* The summaries for the other three cases, and the blank rule-synthesis chart itself, are not present in the file provided. I can't complete the chart or synthesize a rule across four cases without inventing case facts I don't actually have. Below is the rule that can be drawn from Goddard alone; the synthesized rule would need to account for the other three cases once they're available.

**Rule-synthesis chart (partial — 1 of 4 cases available):**

| Case | Key Facts | Holding | Principle/Rule Extracted |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Goddard v. Boston & M. R. R. Co.*, 60 N.E. 486 (Mass. 1901) | Plaintiff slipped on a banana peel on a train station platform with many passengers passing through; no evidence of how long the peel had been there before the fall. | Plaintiff could not recover. | A landowner/occupier is not liable for a slipping hazard left by a third party unless the plaintiff produces evidence of how long the hazard was present — i.e., evidence sufficient to show the defendant had (or should have had) notice of the hazard in time to remove it. |
| Case 2 | *not provided in attached document* | — | — |
| Case 3 | *not provided in attached document* | — | — |
| Case 4 | *not provided in attached document* | — | — |

**What is the rule from *Goddard v. Boston*?**

A plaintiff cannot recover for a slip-and-fall caused by a foreign substance (here, a banana peel) left on a defendant's premises by a third party unless the plaintiff comes forward with evidence establishing how long the substance had been on the ground. Because the mere presence of the hazard, standing alone, does not show the defendant had actual or constructive notice of it, the plaintiff bears the burden of producing some evidence of duration (e.g., the condition of the object itself, testimony about inspection or cleaning intervals) from which a factfinder could infer the defendant had a reasonable opportunity to discover and remove the hazard before the injury occurred. Without that evidence, the claim fails as a matter of law, regardless of how many people were on the premises or how obviously hazardous the substance was.

## Exercise 7.2.1: Identifying the Parts of a Case Illustration

**Question 1: Were both case illustrations complete? If not, identify what was missing in each and how the missing parts might affect a reader's understanding.**

Neither illustration is fully complete against the five required parts (hook, facts, holding, reasoning, transition).

*Sheirod illustration* — It has facts (residence vacant a year, furnished, utilities operable), a three-factor test, a holding (dwelling, "temporary absence"), and reasoning (suitable for "overnight accommodations"). What it lacks is an opening **hook**: a topic sentence stating the legal proposition the case stands for *before* diving into the facts. The paragraph opens with "In Sheirod, a private residence was vacant for a year..." — pure narrative — rather than something like "A structure does not lose its status as a dwelling merely because it sits temporarily unoccupied, so long as it remains suitable for overnight habitation." Without that framing sentence, the reader has to read through the entire fact recitation before learning why the case is being cited at all, which slows comprehension and forces the reader to reconstruct the relevance retroactively.

*Quattlebaum illustration* — It has a transition ("In contrast"), facts (school, fifth-floor offices, bed and chair, occasional overnight stay), and a holding (not a dwelling). What it's missing is developed **reasoning** that actually applies the Sheirod factors to these facts. The sentence "The Court considered the Sheirod factors and the nature of how the structure was 'usually occupied'" *names* the factors instead of *applying* them — it never explains, for instance, whether there was any "intent to return" analysis for a school, or why an occasional overnight stay on the office bed didn't satisfy the "could have been occupied overnight" factor the way the vacant house did in Sheirod. The final quote ("customary indicia of a residence") is dropped in without connecting it back to specific facts (no kitchen, no permanent residents, use limited to work hours, etc.). Because the reasoning is conclusory, the reader cannot see *why* a bed and chair used for occasional overnight stays fails the test that a furnished, utility-equipped, unoccupied house passes — which is precisely the comparison a reader needs in order to apply either case to a new set of facts (like the treehouse).

**Question 2: What does the transition "in contrast" signify? Was the hook in the second case illustration effective?**

"In contrast" signals to the reader that the case about to be discussed reaches the *opposite* result from the case just discussed — it primes the reader to expect a distinguishing fact pattern and a different outcome on the "dwelling" question, which is useful for orienting the reader within the rule-synthesis structure (one case marking one end of the spectrum, the next marking the other).

The "hook" in the second illustration — effectively just "in contrast, in Quattlebaum, the Court came to the opposite conclusion" — is not effective as a hook. A good hook states the *legal principle* the case illustrates, not merely that the result differs. This sentence tells the reader *that* the outcome is different without telling the reader *why* in legal terms (e.g., "occasional overnight use of a room within a nonresidential building does not convert that room into a dwelling"). Because the sentence conveys only an outcome and not a proposition of law, the reader is left waiting until the end of the paragraph to understand the substantive distinction between Sheirod and Quattlebaum, which undercuts the orienting function a hook is supposed to serve.

---

## Exercise 7.2.2: Evaluating Case Illustrations for Effectiveness

**1.** *"The Picaroni court held that burglary of a garage was not burglary of an inhabited dwelling house."*

**Not effective.** This is a bare holding with no facts and no reasoning. It doesn't tell the reader *what kind* of garage (attached or detached, how situated relative to the house), so the reader has no basis for comparing it to Molly Izo's she-shed. A holding stated in isolation like this risks being read too broadly (as if *no* garage, ever, can be part of a dwelling) when the actual force of the holding depends entirely on facts the reader never gets to see.

**2.** *"...affirmed Anthony Picaroni's conviction for burglarizing the contents of a poorly lit garage, including two crates of dishes later found in his truck, and rejected Mr. Picaroni's argument that his conviction... was inconsistent with his acquittal for burglarizing the main house, because the two crimes were not identical."*

**Not effective.** This illustration is packed with facts, but they're the wrong facts — the lighting in the garage, the crates of dishes, and the truck are immaterial to whether a garage counts as part of an "inhabited dwelling house." Worse, the substantive point being illustrated (inconsistent-verdicts is not a valid defense because the crimes charged were legally distinct) answers a different legal question altogether — a procedural argument about verdict consistency, not the structural question of what makes a building part of a dwelling. As applied to Dolich, this illustration gives the prosecutor nothing useful and would confuse a reader trying to evaluate the she-shed issue.

**3.** *"...burglary of a structure that is not attached to a residence does not qualify as burglary of an inhabited dwelling house... the garage and the house were two unconnected, adjacent buildings, separated by a cement walkway."*

**Effective.** This illustration opens with the governing principle (hook), then supplies the legally significant fact — non-attachment, evidenced by a *mere* adjacent walkway rather than a physical connection — and ties that fact directly to the holding. This gives the reader exactly what's needed to compare against Izo's she-shed, which likewise is not attached to the house and sits 15 feet away, connected only by a covered walkway rather than any interior connection. A reader can immediately see the analogy this illustration invites.

**4.** *"...the Cook court held that a building, which is an attached and integral part of a house, can qualify as 'an inhabited dwelling house.'"*

**Not effective**, for the same reason as #1 — it's a conclusory holding with no facts about *what made* the structure "attached and integral" (interior door, shared wall, shared roofline, etc.). Without those facts, the reader cannot tell whether Izo's she-shed — which is on a trailer and physically separate from the house — comes anywhere close to whatever made the Cook structure "integral."

**5.** *"...affirmed Robert Cook's conviction for an early morning burglary of two chairs, a clock radio, and a tool box from the garage and patio... because the garage and patio... qualified as part of the inhabited dwelling house under the common law burglary rule."*

**Not effective.** The time of the burglary and the specific items stolen (chairs, clock radio, tool box) are immaterial to the attachment question. And the stated reasoning — the garage/patio qualified "because" they qualified — is circular; it restates the holding rather than explaining it. A reader gets facts, but not the *legally significant* facts (how the garage/patio physically related to the house), so this illustration can't do the comparative work needed for the she-shed analysis.

**6.** *"...the term 'inhabited dwelling house' includes any structure that is an attached and integral part of a house... neither the garage nor the patio were structures separate from the main house but rather 'they [were] an integral part of the [victim's] residence'... 'simply one room of several which together compose[d] the dwelling especially where the garage can be reached through an inside door connecting it to the rest of the residence.'"*

**Effective.** This is the most complete illustration of the six: it states the rule up front (hook), gives the legally significant fact that drove the outcome (an *interior door* physically connecting the garage to the rest of the house, making it functionally "one room" of the residence), states the holding, and quotes the court's reasoning. This gives a reader a precise point of comparison for the she-shed: unlike Cook's garage, Izo's she-shed has no interior door or physical connection to the house at all — it's a separate, movable trailer-mounted structure reached only by an exterior covered walkway. The specificity of this illustration is exactly what lets the prosecutor draw (or the defense rebut) that distinction credibly.

**Overall pattern across all six:** the effective illustrations (#3 and #6) share the same structure — governing principle stated first, then the *one or two facts that actually drove the court's attachment analysis*, then the holding tied back to those facts. The ineffective ones either omit facts entirely (#1, #4), include facts that are vivid but legally irrelevant (#2, #5), or substitute a conclusion for reasoning (#5). Applied to Dolich, the she-shed's facts — unattached, 15 feet from the house, reached by an exterior covered walkway rather than an interior door, mounted on a trailer — line up much more closely with Picaroni (illustration #3) than with Cook (illustration #6), which suggests the she-shed likely falls outside "an inhabited dwelling house," while the main house burglary count is not in question.

**Rule: R2 § 45 - Option Contract Created by Part Performance or** **Tender**

- **Source**: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 45
- **Document**: R2 §§ 45, 87(2), and 90
- **Statement**: An option contract is created when the offeree begins or tenders the invited performance in response to an offer that invites acceptance through performance rather than a promise.
- **Legal Question**: When is an option contract formed by an offeree's performance?
- **Requirements**:

1. The offer must invite acceptance by performance.
2. The offeree must begin or tender the invited performance.

- **Application**: Courts or parties invoke this rule to determine if an offeror is bound by an option contract due to the offeree's actions.
- **Exceptions**: If the offeror reserves the right to revoke after performance has begun, the promise does not create an option contract.

**Rule: R2 § 87 - Option Contract**

- **Source**: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 87
- **Document**: R2 §§ 45, 87(2), and 90
- **Statement**: An offer is binding as an option contract if it is in writing and signed by the offeror with a stated consideration, or if it induces substantial action or forbearance from the offeree.
- **Legal Question**: Under what circumstances can an offer be enforced as an option contract?
- **Requirements**:

1. The offer must be in writing and signed by the offeror with recited consideration, proposing a fair exchange within a reasonable time.
2. The offer must induce substantial action or forbearance that the offeror reasonably expects.

- **Application**: Used to assess the binding nature of offers that induce reliance before acceptance.
- **Exceptions**: None specified in the section; however, the enforceability can depend on the extent of the reliance.

**Rule: R2 § 90 - Promise Reasonably Inducing Action or** **Forbearance**

- **Source**: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90
- **Document**: R2 §§ 45, 87(2), and 90
- **Statement**: A promise is binding if it induces substantial action or forbearance and enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice, particularly in cases of charitable subscriptions or marriage settlements.
- **Legal Question**: When is a promise enforceable in the absence of a formal contract?
- **Requirements**:

1. The promisor must reasonably expect the promise to induce action or forbearance.
2. The promise must induce such action or forbearance.
3. Injustice can only be avoided by enforcement of the promise.

- **Application**: Courts apply this rule to determine whether non-contractual promises should be enforced due to reliance.
- **Exceptions**: Charitable subscriptions and marriage settlements bind even if reliance is not proven.

**Important Distinctions**

- Offer vs. invitation to make an offer: An offer indicates a willingness to enter a contract, while an invitation to make an offer merely invites parties to propose terms for a contract.
- Offer vs. preliminary negotiation: An offer aims to create a contractual obligation, while preliminary negotiations are discussions that express interest without intent to create a binding agreement.
- Revocation vs. rejection: Revocation is the withdrawal of an offer by the offeror, while rejection is an offeree's refusal to accept the offer.
- Acceptance vs. counteroffer: Acceptance is an agreement to the terms of an offer, while a counteroffer alters the terms and constitutes a new offer.
- Promise vs. performance: A promise is a commitment to do something in the future, whereas performance refers to the execution of that commitment.
- Bilateral vs. unilateral contract: A bilateral contract involves mutual promises, while a unilateral contract is formed when one party makes a promise in exchange for an act.
- Reliance vs. consideration: Reliance refers to actions taken based on a promise, while consideration is something of value exchanged between parties to support a contract.

**Example**: An individual offers a reward for information leading to the arrest of a criminal. A person provides helpful information believing the reward will be paid → The offer induces action (giving information), thus creating an option contract under § 87 if the offer meets the requirements → The individual may be entitled to the reward due to reliance. **Added Hypothetical (not in the reading)**: A contractor offers to build a deck for a homeowner and indicates that starting the work will secure the price offered. The homeowner begins construction → An option contract is formed under § 45 due to the homeowner's beginning performance → The contractor is bound to the price unless he reserved the right to revoke.

**Important Terms** **Option Contract**

- **Meaning**: A contract that binds the offeror to keep an offer open for a specific time in exchange for consideration.
- **Why it matters**: It prevents the offeror from revoking the offer during the option period, affording the offeree time to consider acceptance. **Performance**
- **Meaning**: The execution of the obligations under a contract or offer.
- **Why it matters**: Initiating or completing performance can establish enforceable rights and obligations.

**How the Rules Fit Together**
Rules § 45, § 87, and § 90 interact in establishing when a promise or offer is binding. § 45 outlines how part performance creates an option contract when tied to an invitation for acceptance. § 87 elaborates on the binding nature of offers to induce action or forbearance. § 90 emphasizes enforcement of promises that induce reliance, particularly within informal agreements.

**What I Need to Know**

1. Option contracts can arise from the commencement of invited performance
2. Requirements for binding option contracts include written offers with consideration or substantial reliance
3. Charitable subscriptions may bind promises without reliance proof
4. Distinction between offers and invitations affects enforceability
5. Understanding promises versus performance is crucial in assessing binding nature
6. Recognize how these rules interconnect in considering reliance and contractual obligations

Rule: R2 § 45 - Option Contract Created by Part Performance or Tender
  • Source: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 45
  • Document: R2 §§ 45, 87(2), and 90
  • Statement: An option contract is created when the offeree begins or tenders the invited performance in response to an offer that invites acceptance through performance rather than a promise.
  • Legal Question: When is an option contract formed by an offeree's performance?
  • Requirements:
  1. The offer must invite acceptance by performance.
  2. The offeree must begin or tender the invited performance.
  • Application: Courts or parties invoke this rule to determine if an offeror is bound by an option contract due to the offeree's actions.
  • Exceptions: If the offeror reserves the right to revoke after performance has begun, the promise does not create an option contract.

Rule: R2 § 87 - Option Contract
  • Source: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 87
  • Document: R2 §§ 45, 87(2), and 90
  • Statement: An offer is binding as an option contract if it is in writing and signed by the offeror with a stated consideration, or if it induces substantial action or forbearance from the offeree.
  • Legal Question: Under what circumstances can an offer be enforced as an option contract?
  • Requirements:
  1. The offer must be in writing and signed by the offeror with recited consideration, proposing a fair exchange within a reasonable time.
  2. The offer must induce substantial action or forbearance that the offeror reasonably expects.
  • Application: Used to assess the binding nature of offers that induce reliance before acceptance.
  • Exceptions: None specified in the section; however, the enforceability can depend on the extent of the reliance.

Rule: R2 § 90 - Promise Reasonably Inducing Action or Forbearance

  • Source: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90
  • Document: R2 §§ 45, 87(2), and 90
  • Statement: A promise is binding if it induces substantial action or forbearance and enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice, particularly in cases of charitable subscriptions or marriage settlements.
  • Legal Question: When is a promise enforceable in the absence of a formal contract?
  • Requirements:
  1. The promisor must reasonably expect the promise to induce action or forbearance.
  2. The promise must induce such action or forbearance.
  3. Injustice can only be avoided by enforcement of the promise.
  • Application: Courts apply this rule to determine whether non-contractual promises should be enforced due to reliance.
  • Exceptions: Charitable subscriptions and marriage settlements bind even if reliance is not proven.

Important Distinctions
  • Offer vs. invitation to make an offer: An offer indicates a willingness to enter a contract, while an invitation to make an offer merely invites parties to propose terms for a contract.
  • Offer vs. preliminary negotiation: An offer aims to create a contractual obligation, while preliminary negotiations are discussions that express interest without intent to create a binding agreement.
  • Revocation vs. rejection: Revocation is the withdrawal of an offer by the offeror, while rejection is an offeree's refusal to accept the offer.
  • Acceptance vs. counteroffer: Acceptance is an agreement to the terms of an offer, while a counteroffer alters the terms and constitutes a new offer.
  • Promise vs. performance: A promise is a commitment to do something in the future, whereas performance refers to the execution of that commitment.
  • Bilateral vs. unilateral contract: A bilateral contract involves mutual promises, while a unilateral contract is formed when one party makes a promise in exchange for an act.
  • Reliance vs. consideration: Reliance refers to actions taken based on a promise, while consideration is something of value exchanged between parties to support a contract.


Example: An individual offers a reward for information leading to the arrest of a criminal. A person provides helpful information believing the reward will be paid → The offer induces action (giving information), thus creating an option contract under § 87 if the offer meets the requirements → The individual may be entitled to the reward due to reliance. Added Hypothetical (not in the reading): A contractor offers to build a deck for a homeowner and indicates that starting the work will secure the price offered. The homeowner begins construction → An option contract is formed under § 45 due to the homeowner's beginning performance → The contractor is bound to the price unless he reserved the right to revoke.

Important Terms Option Contract
  • Meaning: A contract that binds the offeror to keep an offer open for a specific time in exchange for consideration.
  • Why it matters: It prevents the offeror from revoking the offer during the option period, affording the offeree time to consider acceptance. Performance
  • Meaning: The execution of the obligations under a contract or offer.
  • Why it matters: Initiating or completing performance can establish enforceable rights and obligations.

How the Rules Fit Together
Rules § 45, § 87, and § 90 interact in establishing when a promise or offer is binding. § 45 outlines how part performance creates an option contract when tied to an invitation for acceptance. § 87 elaborates on the binding nature of offers to induce action or forbearance. § 90 emphasizes enforcement of promises that induce reliance, particularly within informal agreements.

What I Need to Know

  1. Option contracts can arise from the commencement of invited performance
  2. Requirements for binding option contracts include written offers with consideration or substantial reliance
  3. Charitable subscriptions may bind promises without reliance proof
  4. Distinction between offers and invitations affects enforceability
  5. Understanding promises versus performance is crucial in assessing binding nature
  6. Recognize how these rules interconnect in considering reliance and contractual obligations
