savedReports.content: **Rules** **Rule: Promissory Estoppel—Four Elements** - **Source**: California Court of Appeal holding in Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., quoting Advanced Choices, Inc. v. State Department of Health Services - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: A promissory estoppel claim requires a clear and unambiguous promise, reliance by the promisee, reasonable and foreseeable reliance, and injury caused by that reliance - **Legal Question**: When may a promise be enforced despite the absence of an ordinary contract supported by consideration? - **Requirements**: 1. A promise clear and unambiguous in its terms 2. Reliance by the party to whom the promise is made 3. Reliance that is both reasonable and foreseeable 4. Injury caused by the reliance - **Application**: The doctrine applies when a promisor should reasonably expect a promise to induce action or forbearance, the promise does induce that action or forbearance, and injustice would result if the promise were not enforced - **Exceptions**: The doctrine cannot apply without an actual promise, and the remedy may be limited according to the circumstances rather than necessarily providing every remedy available for an ordinary contract claim **Rule: Clear and Unambiguous Promise** - **Source**: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., applying Garcia v. World Savings, FSB - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: A promise is sufficiently definite when a court can determine the scope of the promisor’s duty and the limits of performance provide a rational basis for assessing damages - **Legal Question**: Is the alleged promise definite enough to identify the duty that was undertaken and determine whether it was breached? - **Requirements**: The promise must be clear and unambiguous in its terms - **Application**: The court examines what the promisor actually promised, rather than demanding that the promise contain every term of a final contract - **Exceptions**: A purported agreement is insufficient when it does not provide a basis for determining the parties’ obligations or whether those obligations were breached; a promise’s conditional nature does not by itself make it unenforceable or ambiguous **Rule: Promise to Negotiate Versus Promise to Make a Loan** **Modification** - **Source**: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A. - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: A promise to negotiate toward a mutually agreeable loan solution is distinct from a promise to make a loan or to offer particular modification terms and may be sufficiently clear for promissory estoppel - **Legal Question**: Does a promise to negotiate require the parties to have already agreed on the terms of the ultimate transaction? - **Requirements**: 1. The alleged promise must concern negotiation toward a possible solution 2. The promise must identify a duty to engage in negotiations 3. The plaintiff must rely on the promise of negotiation rather than on the terms of an unconsummated final agreement - **Application**: The relevant inquiry is whether the promisor negotiated as promised, not whether the parties ultimately reached a modification - **Exceptions**: A promise to make a loan or to enter a final loan modification may be too indefinite if essential terms are missing, as illustrated by the distinction from Laks v. Coast Federal Savings & Loan Association **Rule: Conditional Promises** - **Source**: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., quoting Garcia v. World Savings, FSB - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: A promise does not become unenforceable or ambiguous merely because it is conditional - **Legal Question**: Does attaching a condition to a promise prevent the promise from being sufficiently definite? - **Requirements**: The promise must still identify a sufficiently definite duty once the condition is satisfied - **Application**: The court identifies the condition and then determines whether the promisor undertook a recognizable obligation after the condition occurred - **Exceptions**: A condition cannot cure a promise that otherwise fails to identify any enforceable obligation **Rule: Reasonable and Foreseeable Reliance** - **Source**: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., applying the promissory-estoppel standard quoted from Advanced Choices, Inc. v. State Department of Health Services - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: Reliance must be reasonable and foreseeable, meaning the promisor should reasonably expect the promise to induce the promisee’s action or forbearance and the promisee’s reliance must not be manifestly unreasonable - **Legal Question**: Was it justified and foreseeable for the promisee to act or refrain from acting because of the promise? - **Requirements**: 1. The promise would reasonably be expected to induce action or forbearance 2. The promise actually induced the plaintiff’s action or forbearance 3. The plaintiff’s conduct was not manifestly unreasonable in light of the plaintiff’s intelligence and information - **Application**: The court compares the promised performance with the alternative the plaintiff gave up and asks whether the promise presented a compelling reason for the plaintiff’s choice - **Exceptions**: A hopeful expectation or reliance on a statement on which no reasonable person would rely is insufficient **Rule: Detrimental Reliance and Injury** - **Source**: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A. - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: The plaintiff must be injured by relying on the promise, including by giving up a legally available course of action that could have protected the plaintiff’s interests - **Legal Question**: Did the plaintiff lose a meaningful legal or economic opportunity because of reliance on the promise? - **Requirements**: 1. The plaintiff had an available alternative course of action 2. The plaintiff refrained from pursuing that alternative because of the promise 3. The plaintiff suffered resulting injury - **Application**: Aceves alleged that she gave up conversion from chapter 7 to chapter 13, her husband’s financial assistance for a chapter 13 plan, and opposition to the motion to lift the bankruptcy stay - **Exceptions**: The plaintiff’s allegations are accepted as true at the pleading stage, but the plaintiff must ultimately establish actual detrimental reliance **Rule: Chapter 13 as a Means of Avoiding Foreclosure** - **Source**: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A. and the casebook discussion of bankruptcy - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: Chapter 13 may allow an eligible homeowner in default to cure arrearages over time, reinstate the original loan payments, avoid foreclosure, and retain the home - **Legal Question**: What bankruptcy alternative did Aceves allegedly surrender in reliance on the bank’s promise? - **Requirements**: 1. The debtor must be eligible for chapter 13 relief 2. The debtor must propose and comply with a repayment plan 3. The plan must provide for curing the mortgage default 4. The debtor must make the required payments - **Application**: Aceves alleged that she could have used chapter 13, with her husband’s financial assistance, to save her residence - **Exceptions**: Chapter 13 could reinstate the loan but generally could not modify the rights of a lender secured only by the debtor’s residence under the anti-modification provision described in the reading **Rule: Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 Distinction** - **Source**: Casebook narrative accompanying Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A. - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: Chapter 7 is generally a liquidation proceeding that permits discharge of unpaid debts, while chapter 13 permits an individual with regular income to adjust debts through a repayment plan and potentially retain a home - **Legal Question**: Why was conversion from chapter 7 to chapter 13 significant to Aceves? - **Requirements**: 1. Chapter 7 generally involves liquidation and discharge 2. A debtor who discharges an unpaid home loan cannot keep the home on that basis 3. Chapter 13 may permit cure of arrearages over time 4. Chapter 13 may prevent foreclosure while the debtor complies with the plan - **Application**: Aceves alleged that she abandoned the chapter 13 option because U.S. Bank promised to work with her on reinstatement and modification - **Exceptions**: The reading does not state that chapter 13 guarantees a debtor’s ability to retain the home; it describes chapter 13 as an available means of attempting to do so **Rule: Oral Promises, Consideration, and Estoppel** - **Source**: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., discussing California Civil Code § 1698 - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: An oral promise may support promissory estoppel where the circumstances establish reliance and estoppel, even though the promise lacks ordinary contractual consideration - **Legal Question**: Can an oral promise to postpone foreclosure or negotiate a loan solution be enforced through promissory estoppel? - **Requirements**: The plaintiff must establish the elements of promissory estoppel, including a definite promise, reliance, reasonableness, foreseeability, and injury - **Application**: Aceves alleged that she relied on the bank’s oral promise by giving up chapter 13 relief and not opposing the motion to lift the stay - **Exceptions**: The promise does not necessarily support invalidation of a completed foreclosure, particularly where the plaintiff did not pay the funds needed to reinstate the loan before the sale **Rule: Promissory Estoppel Remedy** - **Source**: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A. - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: A promissory estoppel claim generally entitles the plaintiff to damages available on a breach-of-contract claim, but the remedy may not include voiding a completed trustee’s sale - **Legal Question**: What relief is available when promissory estoppel is established? - **Requirements**: The plaintiff must establish reliance-based injury for which contract-type damages can provide compensation - **Application**: The remedy inquiry is separate from whether the complaint adequately states a promissory estoppel claim - **Exceptions**: In Aceves, promissory estoppel did not provide a basis to void the deed of sale or otherwise invalidate the foreclosure because Aceves had not paid the funds necessary to reinstate the loan before the sale **Rule: Fraud Based on a False Promise** - **Source**: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., applying McClain v. Octagon Plaza, LLC - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: Fraud has elements similar to promissory estoppel but additionally requires a false promise and knowledge of its falsity when made - **Legal Question**: When can a broken promise support a fraud claim rather than only a contract or promissory-estoppel claim? - **Requirements**: 1. A promise was made 2. The promise was false 3. The promisor knew the promise was false when made 4. The plaintiff relied on the promise 5. The plaintiff suffered resulting injury - **Application**: Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank never intended to work with her and made the promise to induce her to forgo further bankruptcy proceedings - **Exceptions**: A mere failure to perform a future promise is not ordinarily fraud unless the promise was false when made because the promisor lacked the intent to perform **Rule: Promissory Fraud** - **Source**: Casebook note accompanying Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., Restatement (Second) of Torts § 530 - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: A representation of the maker’s own intention to do or not do a particular thing is fraudulent if the maker does not have that intention when making the representation - **Legal Question**: Can a promise about future conduct constitute a misrepresentation of a present fact? - **Requirements**: The promisor must lack the stated intention at the time the promise is made - **Application**: The alleged promise to negotiate may be treated as a present misrepresentation of U.S. Bank’s existing intention to negotiate - **Exceptions**: A later breach alone does not establish promissory fraud; the lack of intent to perform must exist when the promise is made **Rule: Restatement (Second) § 90** - **Source**: Casebook discussion of the Restatement (Second) view of promissory estoppel - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: Promissory estoppel generally enforces a promise when reliance makes nonenforcement unjust, and the remedy may be limited as justice requires - **Legal Question**: How does the Restatement formulate the reliance principle and its remedial flexibility? - **Requirements**: 1. A promise 2. Reliance by the promisee or a third person 3. Reliance that the promisor should reasonably expect 4. Action or forbearance induced by the promise 5. Enforcement necessary to avoid injustice - **Application**: The section explains the broader doctrinal basis for enforcing promises such as the bank’s promise in Aceves - **Exceptions**: The remedy is not automatically full expectation damages and may be limited as justice requires; charitable subscriptions may be enforced without detrimental reliance under the revised provision discussed in the reading **Rule: Bankruptcy Protection and Creditor Interests** - **Source**: Casebook discussion accompanying Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A. - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: Bankruptcy law balances a debtor’s need for a fresh start or reorganization against protections for creditors and restrictions on bad-faith use of bankruptcy - **Legal Question**: Why can a debtor’s decision to seek chapter 13 protection be legally significant even when a creditor views the filing as abusive? - **Requirements**: The debtor must assert a form of relief authorized by bankruptcy law and comply with applicable statutory requirements - **Application**: The casebook emphasizes that a creditor’s disagreement with a debtor’s use of chapter 13 does not itself establish abuse when the debtor is asserting a statutory right - **Exceptions**: The reading recognizes that bankruptcy law contains provisions protecting creditors from bad-faith use of the process **Rule: Promissory Estoppel in Commercial and Other Contexts** - **Source**: Casebook narrative discussing the development of promissory estoppel - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Statement**: Promissory estoppel has been applied to a wide variety of commercial promises, but courts deny recovery when no enforceable promise exists or detrimental reliance is not established - **Legal Question**: Is promissory estoppel limited to family, charitable, or residential settings? - **Requirements**: The ordinary requirements of promise, reliance, reasonableness, foreseeability, and injury remain applicable - **Application**: The reading gives examples involving confidentiality, homeowners’ association obligations, commissions, and continued services - **Exceptions**: Courts may deny recovery when the promise is absent, the promise is insufficiently definite, or the plaintiff fails to show detrimental reliance **Case Narrative** Claudia Aceves, a married homeowner and borrower, obtained an $845,000 loan from Option One Mortgage Corporation on April 20, 1. The loan was secured by a deed of trust on her residence. It had an initial interest rate of 6.35 percent, an initial monthly payment of $4,857.09, a 30-year term, and an adjustable rate after the first two years. On March 25, 2008, Option One transferred its entire interest under the deed of trust to U.S. Bank, acting as trustee for the certificateholders of a mortgage-backed securities trust. U.S. Bank later substituted Quality Loan Service Corporation as trustee under the deed of trust By January 2008, Aceves could no longer afford the monthly payments. On March 26, 2008, Quality Loan Service recorded a notice of default and election to sell under the deed of trust. Aceves then filed for chapter 7 bankruptcy protection, which automatically stayed the foreclosure proceedings. U.S. Bank told Aceves that once the loan was out of bankruptcy, the bank would work with her on reinstating and modifying the mortgage. The bank asked her to submit documents for consideration Aceves planned to convert her chapter 7 case to chapter 13 and rely on her husband’s financial resources to save the home. Chapter 7 generally permits a debtor to discharge unpaid debts but does not allow the debtor to keep a home by discharging the home loan. Chapter 13 could have allowed Aceves to cure the mortgage arrearages over time, avoid foreclosure, and retain the home. U.S. Bank moved in bankruptcy court to lift the automatic stay so it could proceed with a nonjudicial foreclosure On or about November 12, 2008, counsel for American Home Mortgage Servicing, the company servicing the loan, wrote to Aceves’s bankruptcy attorney and asked for written consent to contact Aceves directly to explore loss-mitigation possibilities. Aceves then contacted American Home’s counsel but was told that the company could not speak with her before the motion to lift the stay was granted. Relying on U.S. Bank’s promise to work with her, Aceves did not oppose the motion to lift the stay, did not convert to chapter 13, and did not rely on her husband’s financial assistance to develop a chapter 13 plan The bankruptcy court lifted the stay on December 4, 2008. On December 9, U.S. Bank scheduled the home for public auction on January 9, 2009, even though neither U.S. Bank nor American Home had begun the promised discussions. Aceves sent documents concerning reinstatement and modification on December 10. On December 23, American Home told her that a negotiator would contact her by January 13, four days after the scheduled auction. On December 29, a negotiator told Aceves to forget about assistance because the file had been discharged in bankruptcy. On January 2, 2009, the negotiator admitted that American Home had mistakenly believed the loan had been discharged and said the company would reconsider a loss-mitigation proposal On January 8, the day before the auction, the negotiator told Aceves’s bankruptcy attorney that the loan balance was $965,926.22, the new monthly payment would exceed $7,200, and a $6,500 deposit had to be sent immediately by Western Union. The negotiator refused to provide those terms in writing, and Aceves did not accept them. On January 9, 2009, the home was sold at a trustee’s sale to U.S. Bank. U.S. Bank served Aceves with a three-day notice to vacate on February 11 and later filed an unlawful detainer action. Aceves and her husband apparently vacated the residence during those eviction proceedings Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank never intended to work with her and made the promise only to induce her to abandon further bankruptcy proceedings, allowing the bank to lift the stay and foreclose. She sued U.S. Bank seeking relief including damages and remedies concerning the trustee’s sale and deed of sale **Cases** **Case Name: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., California Court of** **Appeal, 2011, Mallano, P.J.** - **Document**: CB pp 243-253 - **Course**: Contracts - **Facts** - Plaintiff Claudia Aceves was a married homeowner who borrowed $845,000 from Option One Mortgage Corporation on April 20, 2006 - The loan was secured by a deed of trust on her residence and carried an initial interest rate of 6.35 percent - The initial monthly payments were $4,857.09, the loan term was 30 years, and the rate became adjustable after two years - U.S. Bank acquired Option One’s entire interest under the deed of trust on March 25, 2008 - Quality Loan Service Corporation was substituted as trustee under the deed of trust - Aceves could no longer afford the payments by January 2008 - Quality Loan Service recorded a notice of default and election to sell on March 26, 2008 - Aceves filed chapter 7 bankruptcy, triggering an automatic stay of foreclosure - U.S. Bank told Aceves that once the loan was out of bankruptcy, it would work with her on mortgage reinstatement and loan modification - Aceves intended to convert to chapter 13 and use her husband’s financial resources to save the home - U.S. Bank moved to lift the bankruptcy stay - Counsel for American Home Mortgage Servicing asked Aceves’s attorney to permit direct contact with Aceves to explore loss mitigation - Aceves relied on the bank’s promise by not opposing the motion to lift the stay, not converting to chapter 13, and not relying on her husband’s financial assistance to formulate a chapter 13 plan - The bankruptcy court lifted the stay on December 4, 2008 - U.S. Bank scheduled the home for auction on January 9, 2009, without first beginning the promised negotiations - American Home delayed contact, mistakenly treated the loan as discharged, and eventually proposed undocumented and immediate payment terms on January 8, one day before the auction - Aceves did not accept the proposed terms - U.S. Bank purchased the home at the trustee’s sale on January 9, 2009 - U.S. Bank later served Aceves with a notice to vacate and filed an unlawful detainer action - Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank never intended to negotiate and made the promise to induce her to abandon further bankruptcy relief - **Procedural Posture**: - Superior Court of California, County of Los Angeles: sustained U.S. Bank’s demurrer without leave to amend and entered judgment for U.S. Bank on Aceves’s claims - Appeal of right: Plaintiff-Appellant Aceves sought review in the California Court of Appeal on the grounds that her promissory-estoppel and other claims were adequately pleaded and should not have been dismissed on demurrer - California Court of Appeal: Plaintiff-Appellant Aceves is the appellant; Defendant-Appellee U.S. Bank is the appellee - **Issue**: Whether Aceves adequately pleaded promissory estoppel and fraud based on U.S. Bank’s alleged promise to work with her on reinstating and modifying the loan? - **Holding**: The California Court of Appeal held that Aceves adequately stated claims for promissory estoppel and fraud, although promissory estoppel did not provide a basis for voiding the completed foreclosure - **Rule**: Promissory Estoppel—Four Elements: A plaintiff must show a clear and unambiguous promise, reliance, reasonable and foreseeable reliance, and injury caused by that reliance - **Reasoning**: - The appeals court treated the complaint’s factual allegations as true at the demurrer stage - U.S. Bank’s alleged promise to work with Aceves on reinstating and modifying the loan was sufficiently clear and unambiguous - The promise concerned negotiation toward a mutually agreeable solution, not a promise that U.S. Bank would necessarily grant a particular modification - The bank either did or did not engage in the promised negotiations, so the duty was sufficiently definite to permit evaluation of breach - Aceves relied on the promise by declining to convert her chapter 7 case to chapter 13 - She also relied by not using her husband’s financial assistance to develop a chapter 13 plan and by not opposing the motion to lift the stay - Reliance was reasonable and foreseeable because chapter 13 could have allowed Aceves to cure arrearages, reinstate the loan, and avoid foreclosure, while negotiation with the bank could potentially have produced additional benefits through loan modification - The complaint alleged that Aceves could have saved the home with her husband’s financial assistance, and the bank’s contrary argument was speculation inappropriate at the pleading stage - The alleged injury consisted of giving up chapter 13 protections, including the ability to cure arrearages over a reasonable period and prevent foreclosure - The alleged promise also supported fraud because Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank never intended to negotiate when it made the promise - The court distinguished the existence of a viable claim from the availability of a particular remedy - Because Aceves had not paid the funds needed to reinstate the loan before the foreclosure, promissory estoppel did not justify voiding the trustee’s deed or invalidating the sale - **Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments**: - Aceves argued that U.S. Bank made a clear promise to work with her on reinstating and modifying the loan - She argued that the promise induced her not to convert her chapter 7 case to chapter 13 - She argued that she also gave up her husband’s financial assistance and did not oppose the bank’s motion to lift the stay - She contended that her reliance was reasonable because chapter 13 could have allowed her to save the home - She argued that the bank never intended to negotiate and therefore committed fraud by making a false promise - She argued that her remaining claims and requested remedies should also survive the demurrer - **Defendant/Appellant's Arguments**: - U.S. Bank argued that its alleged promise was too indefinite to support promissory estoppel - The bank relied on the argument that a promise to negotiate did not identify the essential terms of a loan modification - U.S. Bank argued that it had offered Aceves a loan modification through the January 8 proposal - The bank argued that an oral promise to postpone a payment or foreclosure was unenforceable - U.S. Bank argued that Aceves could not have afforded a chapter 13 plan - The bank characterized Aceves’s bankruptcy conduct as bad faith - U.S. Bank argued that promissory estoppel could not support the requested relief - **Disposition**: The California Court of Appeal reversed the order and judgment insofar as they dismissed the promissory-estoppel and fraud claims and affirmed in all other respects - **Importance**: Aceves illustrates that promissory estoppel can enforce a promise to negotiate even when the parties never reach a final modified contract. It is especially important for distinguishing a promise to negotiate from a promise to make a loan, identifying reliance on a surrendered legal option, separating liability from remedy, and showing how the same facts can support promissory fraud when the promisor allegedly lacked intent to perform from the outset **Definitions** **Promissory Estoppel** - **Definition**: A doctrine that may enforce a promise when the promise induces reasonable and foreseeable reliance and nonenforcement would result in injustice - **Significance**: Aceves used the doctrine to argue that the bank should be liable for inducing her to abandon chapter 13 bankruptcy relief - **Distinction**: Promissory estoppel does not require the plaintiff to prove a completed bargain in the same way as an ordinary contract claim **Promise to Negotiate** - **Definition**: A promise to engage in discussions or negotiations in an effort to reach mutually agreeable terms - **Significance**: U.S. Bank allegedly promised to work with Aceves on reinstatement and modification, and the appellate court treated that promise as sufficiently definite - **Distinction**: It differs from a promise to make a loan or grant a particular modification because the promisor undertakes negotiation rather than a guaranteed final result **Reinstatement** - **Definition**: Restoration of a defaulted loan to its predefault condition through payment or cure of arrearages - **Significance**: Reinstatement was one of the subjects of U.S. Bank’s alleged promise and one of the forms of relief potentially available through chapter 13 - **Distinction**: Reinstatement cures the default but does not necessarily modify the principal, payment amount, interest rate, or duration of the loan **Loan Modification** - **Definition**: A change to the existing loan’s terms, such as reducing regular payments or extending the loan’s life - **Significance**: Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank promised to negotiate a modification in addition to reinstatement - **Distinction**: The promise to negotiate a modification was enforceable as a promise to negotiate even though no final modification was reached **Detrimental Reliance** - **Definition**: Reliance that causes injury because the promisee takes action or gives up an alternative course of action - **Significance**: Aceves allegedly gave up conversion to chapter 13, her husband’s financial assistance, and opposition to lifting the stay - **Distinction**: Reliance must be more than a hopeful expectation and must be reasonable in the circumstances **Demurrer** - **Definition**: The procedural mechanism used in the case to challenge whether the complaint adequately states a legally sufficient claim - **Significance**: The trial court sustained U.S. Bank’s demurrer, while the appellate court concluded that the promissory-estoppel and fraud allegations were legally sufficient - **Distinction**: The demurrer stage concerns the sufficiency of pleaded allegations rather than whether the plaintiff will ultimately prevail at trial **Automatic Stay** - **Definition**: The stay imposed by filing bankruptcy that halts specified collection and foreclosure activity - **Significance**: Aceves’s chapter 7 filing initially stayed U.S. Bank’s foreclosure, and Aceves relied on the bank’s promise when she did not oppose lifting the stay - **Distinction**: The stay temporarily restricts foreclosure activity; it does not itself permanently resolve the mortgage debt or guarantee retention of the property **Chapter 7 Bankruptcy** - **Definition**: A bankruptcy proceeding generally characterized in the reading as liquidation and discharge of unpaid debts - **Significance**: Aceves initially filed chapter 7 and considered converting to chapter 13 - **Distinction**: Chapter 7 differs from chapter 13 because chapter 13 provides a repayment structure that may allow an eligible homeowner to cure mortgage arrearages and retain the home **Chapter 13 Bankruptcy** - **Definition**: A bankruptcy proceeding for an individual with regular income that may permit adjustment of debts through a repayment plan - **Significance**: Aceves alleged that chapter 13 could have allowed her to cure arrearages, avoid foreclosure, and save the residence - **Distinction**: Chapter 13 generally requires repayment of the mortgage obligation and, under the anti-modification provision discussed in the reading, may not permit modification of certain rights of a lender secured only by the residence **Promissory Fraud** - **Definition**: Fraud based on a promise made without the present intention to perform - **Significance**: Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank promised to negotiate only to induce her to abandon further bankruptcy proceedings - **Distinction**: The critical issue is the promisor’s intent when the promise was made, not merely the fact that performance later failed **Anti-Modification Provision** - **Definition**: The bankruptcy limitation described in the reading under which 11 U.S.C. § 1322(b)(2) bars a debtor from modifying certain rights of a lender secured only by an interest in the debtor’s residence - **Significance**: It explains why chapter 13 could reinstate Aceves’s loan and permit cure of arrearages but could not necessarily reduce payments or extend the loan’s life - **Distinction**: Reinstatement and cure address a default, while modification changes the lender’s contractual rights or the loan’s payment terms **Nonjudicial Foreclosure** - **Definition**: Foreclosure conducted through the deed-of-trust process rather than through a judicial foreclosure action - **Significance**: U.S. Bank sought to proceed with a nonjudicial foreclosure after obtaining relief from the automatic stay - **Distinction**: The reading focuses on the bank’s promise and Aceves’s reliance, not on a comprehensive comparison between judicial and nonjudicial foreclosure procedures **Trustee’s Sale** - **Definition**: The sale conducted under a deed of trust after default and foreclosure proceedings - **Significance**: U.S. Bank purchased Aceves’s home at the trustee’s sale on January 9, 2009 - **Distinction**: The appellate court allowed the promissory-estoppel and fraud claims to proceed but held that promissory estoppel did not itself provide a basis for voiding the completed sale in the circumstances alleged

Rules Rule: Promissory Estoppel—Four Elements
  • Source: California Court of Appeal holding in <i>Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A.</i>, quoting <i>Advanced Choices, Inc. v. State Department of Health Services</i>
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: A promissory estoppel claim requires a clear and unambiguous promise, reliance by the promisee, reasonable and foreseeable reliance, and injury caused by that reliance
  • Legal Question: When may a promise be enforced despite the absence of an ordinary contract supported by consideration?
  • Requirements:
  1. A promise clear and unambiguous in its terms
  2. Reliance by the party to whom the promise is made
  3. Reliance that is both reasonable and foreseeable
  4. Injury caused by the reliance
  • Application: The doctrine applies when a promisor should reasonably expect a promise to induce action or forbearance, the promise does induce that action or forbearance, and injustice would result if the promise were not enforced
  • Exceptions: The doctrine cannot apply without an actual promise, and the remedy may be limited according to the circumstances rather than necessarily providing every remedy available for an ordinary contract claim

Rule: Clear and Unambiguous Promise

  • Source: <i>Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A.</i>, applying <i>Garcia v. World Savings, FSB</i>
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: A promise is sufficiently definite when a court can determine the scope of the promisor’s duty and the limits of performance provide a rational basis for assessing damages
  • Legal Question: Is the alleged promise definite enough to identify the duty that was undertaken and determine whether it was breached?
  • Requirements: The promise must be clear and unambiguous in its terms
  • Application: The court examines what the promisor actually promised, rather than demanding that the promise contain every term of a final contract
  • Exceptions: A purported agreement is insufficient when it does not provide a basis for determining the parties’ obligations or whether those obligations were breached; a promise’s conditional nature does not by itself make it unenforceable or ambiguous

Rule: Promise to Negotiate Versus Promise to Make a Loan Modification
  • Source: <i>Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A.</i>
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: A promise to negotiate toward a mutually agreeable loan solution is distinct from a promise to make a loan or to offer particular modification terms and may be sufficiently clear for promissory estoppel
  • Legal Question: Does a promise to negotiate require the parties to have already agreed on the terms of the ultimate transaction?
  • Requirements:
  1. The alleged promise must concern negotiation toward a possible solution
  2. The promise must identify a duty to engage in negotiations
  3. The plaintiff must rely on the promise of negotiation rather than on the terms of an unconsummated final agreement
  • Application: The relevant inquiry is whether the promisor negotiated as promised, not whether the parties ultimately reached a modification
  • Exceptions: A promise to make a loan or to enter a final loan modification may be too indefinite if essential terms are missing, as illustrated by the distinction from <i>Laks v. Coast Federal Savings & Loan Association</i>


Rule: Conditional Promises
  • Source: <i>Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A.</i>, quoting <i>Garcia v. World Savings, FSB</i>
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: A promise does not become unenforceable or ambiguous merely because it is conditional
  • Legal Question: Does attaching a condition to a promise prevent the promise from being sufficiently definite?
  • Requirements: The promise must still identify a sufficiently definite duty once the condition is satisfied
  • Application: The court identifies the condition and then determines whether the promisor undertook a recognizable obligation after the condition occurred
  • Exceptions: A condition cannot cure a promise that otherwise fails to identify any enforceable obligation

Rule: Reasonable and Foreseeable Reliance

  • Source: <i>Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A.</i>, applying the promissory-estoppel standard quoted from <i>Advanced Choices, Inc. v. State Department of Health Services</i>
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: Reliance must be reasonable and foreseeable, meaning the promisor should reasonably expect the promise to induce the promisee’s action or forbearance and the promisee’s reliance must not be manifestly unreasonable
  • Legal Question: Was it justified and foreseeable for the promisee to act or refrain from acting because of the promise?
  • Requirements:
  1. The promise would reasonably be expected to induce action or forbearance
  2. The promise actually induced the plaintiff’s action or forbearance
  3. The plaintiff’s conduct was not manifestly unreasonable in light of the plaintiff’s intelligence and information
  • Application: The court compares the promised performance with the alternative the plaintiff gave up and asks whether the promise presented a compelling reason for the plaintiff’s choice
  • Exceptions: A hopeful expectation or reliance on a statement on which no reasonable person would rely is insufficient

Rule: Detrimental Reliance and Injury

  • Source: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A.
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: The plaintiff must be injured by relying on the promise, including by giving up a legally available course of action that could have protected the plaintiff’s interests
  • Legal Question: Did the plaintiff lose a meaningful legal or economic opportunity because of reliance on the promise?
  • Requirements:
  1. The plaintiff had an available alternative course of action
  2. The plaintiff refrained from pursuing that alternative because of the promise
  3. The plaintiff suffered resulting injury
  • Application: Aceves alleged that she gave up conversion from chapter 7 to chapter 13, her husband’s financial assistance for a chapter 13 plan, and opposition to the motion to lift the bankruptcy stay
  • Exceptions: The plaintiff’s allegations are accepted as true at the pleading stage, but the plaintiff must ultimately establish actual detrimental reliance

Rule: Chapter 13 as a Means of Avoiding Foreclosure

  • Source: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A. and the casebook discussion of bankruptcy
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: Chapter 13 may allow an eligible homeowner in default to cure arrearages over time, reinstate the original loan payments, avoid foreclosure, and retain the home
  • Legal Question: What bankruptcy alternative did Aceves allegedly surrender in reliance on the bank’s promise?
  • Requirements:
  1. The debtor must be eligible for chapter 13 relief
  2. The debtor must propose and comply with a repayment plan
  3. The plan must provide for curing the mortgage default
  4. The debtor must make the required payments
  • Application: Aceves alleged that she could have used chapter 13, with her husband’s financial assistance, to save her residence
  • Exceptions: Chapter 13 could reinstate the loan but generally could not modify the rights of a lender secured only by the debtor’s residence under the anti-modification provision described in the reading

Rule: Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 Distinction

  • Source: Casebook narrative accompanying Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A.
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: Chapter 7 is generally a liquidation proceeding that permits discharge of unpaid debts, while chapter 13 permits an individual with regular income to adjust debts through a repayment plan and potentially retain a home
  • Legal Question: Why was conversion from chapter 7 to chapter 13 significant to Aceves?
  • Requirements:
  1. Chapter 7 generally involves liquidation and discharge
  2. A debtor who discharges an unpaid home loan cannot keep the home on that basis
  3. Chapter 13 may permit cure of arrearages over time
  4. Chapter 13 may prevent foreclosure while the debtor complies with the plan
  • Application: Aceves alleged that she abandoned the chapter 13 option because U.S. Bank promised to work with her on reinstatement and modification
  • Exceptions: The reading does not state that chapter 13 guarantees a debtor’s ability to retain the home; it describes chapter 13 as an available means of attempting to do so

Rule: Oral Promises, Consideration, and Estoppel
  • Source: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., discussing California Civil Code § 1698
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: An oral promise may support promissory estoppel where the circumstances establish reliance and estoppel, even though the promise lacks ordinary contractual consideration
  • Legal Question: Can an oral promise to postpone foreclosure or negotiate a loan solution be enforced through promissory estoppel?
  • Requirements: The plaintiff must establish the elements of promissory estoppel, including a definite promise, reliance, reasonableness, foreseeability, and injury
  • Application: Aceves alleged that she relied on the bank’s oral promise by giving up chapter 13 relief and not opposing the motion to lift the stay
  • Exceptions: The promise does not necessarily support invalidation of a completed foreclosure, particularly where the plaintiff did not pay the funds needed to reinstate the loan before the sale


Rule: Promissory Estoppel Remedy
  • Source: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A.
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: A promissory estoppel claim generally entitles the plaintiff to damages available on a breach-of-contract claim, but the remedy may not include voiding a completed trustee’s sale
  • Legal Question: What relief is available when promissory estoppel is established?
  • Requirements: The plaintiff must establish reliance-based injury for which contract-type damages can provide compensation
  • Application: The remedy inquiry is separate from whether the complaint adequately states a promissory estoppel claim
  • Exceptions: In <i>Aceves</i>, promissory estoppel did not provide a basis to void the deed of sale or otherwise invalidate the foreclosure because Aceves had not paid the funds necessary to reinstate the loan before the sale

Rule: Fraud Based on a False Promise

  • Source: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., applying McClain v. Octagon Plaza, LLC
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: Fraud has elements similar to promissory estoppel but additionally requires a false promise and knowledge of its falsity when made
  • Legal Question: When can a broken promise support a fraud claim rather than only a contract or promissory-estoppel claim?
  • Requirements:
  1. A promise was made
  2. The promise was false
  3. The promisor knew the promise was false when made
  4. The plaintiff relied on the promise
  5. The plaintiff suffered resulting injury
  • Application: Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank never intended to work with her and made the promise to induce her to forgo further bankruptcy proceedings
  • Exceptions: A mere failure to perform a future promise is not ordinarily fraud unless the promise was false when made because the promisor lacked the intent to perform

Rule: Promissory Fraud
  • Source: Casebook note accompanying Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., Restatement (Second) of Torts § 530
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: A representation of the maker’s own intention to do or not do a particular thing is fraudulent if the maker does not have that intention when making the representation
  • Legal Question: Can a promise about future conduct constitute a misrepresentation of a present fact?
  • Requirements: The promisor must lack the stated intention at the time the promise is made
  • Application: The alleged promise to negotiate may be treated as a present misrepresentation of U.S. Bank’s existing intention to negotiate
  • Exceptions: A later breach alone does not establish promissory fraud; the lack of intent to perform must exist when the promise is made


Rule: Restatement (Second) § 90
  • Source: Casebook discussion of the Restatement (Second) view of promissory estoppel
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: Promissory estoppel generally enforces a promise when reliance makes nonenforcement unjust, and the remedy may be limited as justice requires
  • Legal Question: How does the Restatement formulate the reliance principle and its remedial flexibility?
  • Requirements:
  1. A promise
  2. Reliance by the promisee or a third person
  3. Reliance that the promisor should reasonably expect
  4. Action or forbearance induced by the promise
  5. Enforcement necessary to avoid injustice
  • Application: The section explains the broader doctrinal basis for enforcing promises such as the bank’s promise in <i>Aceves</i>
  • Exceptions: The remedy is not automatically full expectation damages and may be limited as justice requires; charitable subscriptions may be enforced without detrimental reliance under the revised provision discussed in the reading

Rule: Bankruptcy Protection and Creditor Interests

  • Source: Casebook discussion accompanying Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A.
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: Bankruptcy law balances a debtor’s need for a fresh start or reorganization against protections for creditors and restrictions on bad-faith use of bankruptcy
  • Legal Question: Why can a debtor’s decision to seek chapter 13 protection be legally significant even when a creditor views the filing as abusive?
  • Requirements: The debtor must assert a form of relief authorized by bankruptcy law and comply with applicable statutory requirements
  • Application: The casebook emphasizes that a creditor’s disagreement with a debtor’s use of chapter 13 does not itself establish abuse when the debtor is asserting a statutory right
  • Exceptions: The reading recognizes that bankruptcy law contains provisions protecting creditors from bad-faith use of the process

Rule: Promissory Estoppel in Commercial and Other Contexts
  • Source: Casebook narrative discussing the development of promissory estoppel
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Statement: Promissory estoppel has been applied to a wide variety of commercial promises, but courts deny recovery when no enforceable promise exists or detrimental reliance is not established
  • Legal Question: Is promissory estoppel limited to family, charitable, or residential settings?
  • Requirements: The ordinary requirements of promise, reliance, reasonableness, foreseeability, and injury remain applicable
  • Application: The reading gives examples involving confidentiality, homeowners’ association obligations, commissions, and continued services
  • Exceptions: Courts may deny recovery when the promise is absent, the promise is insufficiently definite, or the plaintiff fails to show detrimental reliance

Case Narrative

Claudia Aceves, a married homeowner and borrower, obtained an $845,000 loan from Option One Mortgage Corporation on April 20,
  1. The loan was secured by a deed of trust on her residence. It had an initial interest rate of 6.35 percent, an initial monthly payment of $4,857.09, a 30-year term, and an adjustable rate after the first two years. On March 25, 2008, Option One transferred its entire interest under the deed of trust to U.S. Bank, acting as trustee for the certificateholders of a mortgage-backed securities trust. U.S. Bank later substituted Quality Loan Service Corporation as trustee under the deed of trust By January 2008, Aceves could no longer afford the monthly payments. On March 26, 2008, Quality Loan Service recorded a notice of default and election to sell under the deed of trust. Aceves then filed for chapter 7 bankruptcy protection, which automatically stayed the foreclosure proceedings. U.S. Bank told Aceves that once the loan was out of bankruptcy, the bank would work with her on reinstating and modifying the mortgage. The bank asked her to submit documents for consideration Aceves planned to convert her chapter 7 case to chapter 13 and rely on her husband’s financial resources to save the home. Chapter 7 generally permits a debtor to discharge unpaid debts but does not allow the debtor to keep a home by discharging the home loan. Chapter 13 could have allowed Aceves to cure the mortgage arrearages over time, avoid foreclosure, and retain the home. U.S. Bank moved in bankruptcy court to lift the automatic stay so it could proceed with a nonjudicial foreclosure On or about November 12, 2008, counsel for American Home Mortgage Servicing, the company servicing the loan, wrote to Aceves’s bankruptcy attorney and asked for written consent to contact Aceves directly to explore loss-mitigation possibilities. Aceves then contacted American Home’s counsel but was told that the company could not speak with her before the motion to lift the stay was granted. Relying on U.S. Bank’s promise to work with her, Aceves did not oppose the motion to lift the stay, did not convert to chapter 13, and did not rely on her husband’s financial assistance to develop a chapter 13 plan The bankruptcy court lifted the stay on December 4, 2008. On December 9, U.S. Bank scheduled the home for public auction on January 9, 2009, even though neither U.S. Bank nor American Home had begun the promised discussions. Aceves sent documents concerning reinstatement and modification on December 10. On December 23, American Home told her that a negotiator would contact her by January 13, four days after the scheduled auction. On December 29, a negotiator told Aceves to forget about assistance because the file had been discharged in bankruptcy. On January 2, 2009, the negotiator admitted that American Home had mistakenly believed the loan had been discharged and said the company would reconsider a loss-mitigation proposal

On January 8, the day before the auction, the negotiator told Aceves’s bankruptcy attorney that the loan balance was $965,926.22, the new monthly payment would exceed $7,200, and a $6,500 deposit had to be sent immediately by Western Union. The negotiator refused to provide those terms in writing, and Aceves did not accept them. On January 9, 2009, the home was sold at a trustee’s sale to U.S. Bank. U.S. Bank served Aceves with a three-day notice to vacate on February 11 and later filed an unlawful detainer action. Aceves and her husband apparently vacated the residence during those eviction proceedings Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank never intended to work with her and made the promise only to induce her to abandon further bankruptcy proceedings, allowing the bank to lift the stay and foreclose. She sued U.S. Bank seeking relief including damages and remedies concerning the trustee’s sale and deed of sale
Cases Case Name: Aceves v. U.S. Bank, N.A., California Court of Appeal, 2011, Mallano, P.J.
  • Document: CB pp 243-253
  • Course: Contracts

  • Facts
  • Plaintiff Claudia Aceves was a married homeowner who borrowed $845,000 from Option One Mortgage Corporation on April 20, 2006
  • The loan was secured by a deed of trust on her residence and carried an initial interest rate of 6.35 percent
  • The initial monthly payments were $4,857.09, the loan term was 30 years, and the rate became adjustable after two years
  • U.S. Bank acquired Option One’s entire interest under the deed of trust on March 25, 2008
  • Quality Loan Service Corporation was substituted as trustee under the deed of trust
  • Aceves could no longer afford the payments by January 2008
  • Quality Loan Service recorded a notice of default and election to sell on March 26, 2008
  • Aceves filed chapter 7 bankruptcy, triggering an automatic stay of foreclosure
  • U.S. Bank told Aceves that once the loan was out of bankruptcy, it would work with her on mortgage reinstatement and loan modification
  • Aceves intended to convert to chapter 13 and use her husband’s financial resources to save the home
  • U.S. Bank moved to lift the bankruptcy stay
  • Counsel for American Home Mortgage Servicing asked Aceves’s attorney to permit direct contact with Aceves to explore loss mitigation
  • Aceves relied on the bank’s promise by not opposing the motion to lift the stay, not converting to chapter 13, and not relying on her husband’s financial assistance to formulate a chapter 13 plan
  • The bankruptcy court lifted the stay on December 4, 2008
  • U.S. Bank scheduled the home for auction on January 9, 2009, without first beginning the promised negotiations
  • American Home delayed contact, mistakenly treated the loan as discharged, and eventually proposed undocumented and immediate payment terms on January 8, one day before the auction
  • Aceves did not accept the proposed terms
  • U.S. Bank purchased the home at the trustee’s sale on January 9, 2009
  • U.S. Bank later served Aceves with a notice to vacate and filed an unlawful detainer action
  • Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank never intended to negotiate and made the promise to induce her to abandon further bankruptcy relief

  • Procedural Posture:
  • Superior Court of California, County of Los Angeles: sustained U.S. Bank’s demurrer without leave to amend and entered judgment for U.S. Bank on Aceves’s claims
  • Appeal of right: Plaintiff-Appellant Aceves sought review in the California Court of Appeal on the grounds that her promissory-estoppel and other claims were adequately pleaded and should not have been dismissed on demurrer
  • California Court of Appeal: Plaintiff-Appellant Aceves is the appellant; Defendant-Appellee U.S. Bank is the appellee
  • Issue: Whether Aceves adequately pleaded promissory estoppel and fraud based on U.S. Bank’s alleged promise to work with her on reinstating and modifying the loan?
  • Holding: The California Court of Appeal held that Aceves adequately stated claims for promissory estoppel and fraud, although promissory estoppel did not provide a basis for voiding the completed foreclosure
  • Rule: Promissory Estoppel—Four Elements: A plaintiff must show a clear and unambiguous promise, reliance, reasonable and foreseeable reliance, and injury caused by that reliance

  • Reasoning:
  • The appeals court treated the complaint’s factual allegations as true at the demurrer stage
  • U.S. Bank’s alleged promise to work with Aceves on reinstating and modifying the loan was sufficiently clear and unambiguous
  • The promise concerned negotiation toward a mutually agreeable solution, not a promise that U.S. Bank would necessarily grant a particular modification
  • The bank either did or did not engage in the promised negotiations, so the duty was sufficiently definite to permit evaluation of breach
  • Aceves relied on the promise by declining to convert her chapter 7 case to chapter 13
  • She also relied by not using her husband’s financial assistance to develop a chapter 13 plan and by not opposing the motion to lift the stay
  • Reliance was reasonable and foreseeable because chapter 13 could have allowed Aceves to cure arrearages, reinstate the loan, and avoid foreclosure, while negotiation with the bank could potentially have produced additional benefits through loan modification
  • The complaint alleged that Aceves could have saved the home with her husband’s financial assistance, and the bank’s contrary argument was speculation inappropriate at the pleading stage
  • The alleged injury consisted of giving up chapter 13 protections, including the ability to cure arrearages over a reasonable period and prevent foreclosure
  • The alleged promise also supported fraud because Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank never intended to negotiate when it made the promise
  • The court distinguished the existence of a viable claim from the availability of a particular remedy
  • Because Aceves had not paid the funds needed to reinstate the loan before the foreclosure, promissory estoppel did not justify voiding the trustee’s deed or invalidating the sale
  • Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments:
  • Aceves argued that U.S. Bank made a clear promise to work with her on reinstating and modifying the loan
  • She argued that the promise induced her not to convert her chapter 7 case to chapter 13
  • She argued that she also gave up her husband’s financial assistance and did not oppose the bank’s motion to lift the stay
  • She contended that her reliance was reasonable because chapter 13 could have allowed her to save the home
  • She argued that the bank never intended to negotiate and therefore committed fraud by making a false promise
  • She argued that her remaining claims and requested remedies should also survive the demurrer

  • Defendant/Appellant's Arguments:
  • U.S. Bank argued that its alleged promise was too indefinite to support promissory estoppel
  • The bank relied on the argument that a promise to negotiate did not identify the essential terms of a loan modification
  • U.S. Bank argued that it had offered Aceves a loan modification through the January 8 proposal
  • The bank argued that an oral promise to postpone a payment or foreclosure was unenforceable
  • U.S. Bank argued that Aceves could not have afforded a chapter 13 plan
  • The bank characterized Aceves’s bankruptcy conduct as bad faith
  • U.S. Bank argued that promissory estoppel could not support the requested relief
  • Disposition: The California Court of Appeal reversed the order and judgment insofar as they dismissed the promissory-estoppel and fraud claims and affirmed in all other respects
  • Importance: <i>Aceves</i> illustrates that promissory estoppel can enforce a promise to negotiate even when the parties never reach a final modified contract. It is especially important for distinguishing a promise to negotiate from a promise to make a loan, identifying reliance on a surrendered legal option, separating liability from remedy, and showing how the same facts can support promissory fraud when the promisor allegedly lacked intent to perform from the outset

Definitions Promissory Estoppel
  • Definition: A doctrine that may enforce a promise when the promise induces reasonable and foreseeable reliance and nonenforcement would result in injustice
  • Significance: Aceves used the doctrine to argue that the bank should be liable for inducing her to abandon chapter 13 bankruptcy relief
  • Distinction: Promissory estoppel does not require the plaintiff to prove a completed bargain in the same way as an ordinary contract claim

Promise to Negotiate
  • Definition: A promise to engage in discussions or negotiations in an effort to reach mutually agreeable terms

  • Significance: U.S. Bank allegedly promised to work with Aceves on reinstatement and modification, and the appellate court treated that promise as sufficiently definite
  • Distinction: It differs from a promise to make a loan or grant a particular modification because the promisor undertakes negotiation rather than a guaranteed final result

Reinstatement
  • Definition: Restoration of a defaulted loan to its predefault condition through payment or cure of arrearages
  • Significance: Reinstatement was one of the subjects of U.S. Bank’s alleged promise and one of the forms of relief potentially available through chapter 13
  • Distinction: Reinstatement cures the default but does not necessarily modify the principal, payment amount, interest rate, or duration of the loan

Loan Modification
  • Definition: A change to the existing loan’s terms, such as reducing regular payments or extending the loan’s life
  • Significance: Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank promised to negotiate a modification in addition to reinstatement
  • Distinction: The promise to negotiate a modification was enforceable as a promise to negotiate even though no final modification was reached

Detrimental Reliance
  • Definition: Reliance that causes injury because the promisee takes action or gives up an alternative course of action
  • Significance: Aceves allegedly gave up conversion to chapter 13, her husband’s financial assistance, and opposition to lifting the stay
  • Distinction: Reliance must be more than a hopeful expectation and must be reasonable in the circumstances


Demurrer
  • Definition: The procedural mechanism used in the case to challenge whether the complaint adequately states a legally sufficient claim
  • Significance: The trial court sustained U.S. Bank’s demurrer, while the appellate court concluded that the promissory-estoppel and fraud allegations were legally sufficient
  • Distinction: The demurrer stage concerns the sufficiency of pleaded allegations rather than whether the plaintiff will ultimately prevail at trial

Automatic Stay
  • Definition: The stay imposed by filing bankruptcy that halts specified collection and foreclosure activity
  • Significance: Aceves’s chapter 7 filing initially stayed U.S. Bank’s foreclosure, and Aceves relied on the bank’s promise when she did not oppose lifting the stay
  • Distinction: The stay temporarily restricts foreclosure activity; it does not itself permanently resolve the mortgage debt or guarantee retention of the property

Chapter 7 Bankruptcy
  • Definition: A bankruptcy proceeding generally characterized in the reading as liquidation and discharge of unpaid debts
  • Significance: Aceves initially filed chapter 7 and considered converting to chapter 13
  • Distinction: Chapter 7 differs from chapter 13 because chapter 13 provides a repayment structure that may allow an eligible homeowner to cure mortgage arrearages and retain the home

Chapter 13 Bankruptcy
  • Definition: A bankruptcy proceeding for an individual with regular income that may permit adjustment of debts through a repayment plan

  • Significance: Aceves alleged that chapter 13 could have allowed her to cure arrearages, avoid foreclosure, and save the residence
  • Distinction: Chapter 13 generally requires repayment of the mortgage obligation and, under the anti-modification provision discussed in the reading, may not permit modification of certain rights of a lender secured only by the residence

Promissory Fraud
  • Definition: Fraud based on a promise made without the present intention to perform
  • Significance: Aceves alleged that U.S. Bank promised to negotiate only to induce her to abandon further bankruptcy proceedings
  • Distinction: The critical issue is the promisor’s intent when the promise was made, not merely the fact that performance later failed

Anti-Modification Provision
  • Definition: The bankruptcy limitation described in the reading under which 11 U.S.C. § 1322(b)(2) bars a debtor from modifying certain rights of a lender secured only by an interest in the debtor’s residence
  • Significance: It explains why chapter 13 could reinstate Aceves’s loan and permit cure of arrearages but could not necessarily reduce payments or extend the loan’s life
  • Distinction: Reinstatement and cure address a default, while modification changes the lender’s contractual rights or the loan’s payment terms

Nonjudicial Foreclosure
  • Definition: Foreclosure conducted through the deed-of-trust process rather than through a judicial foreclosure action
  • Significance: U.S. Bank sought to proceed with a nonjudicial foreclosure after obtaining relief from the automatic stay
  • Distinction: The reading focuses on the bank’s promise and Aceves’s reliance, not on a comprehensive comparison between judicial and nonjudicial foreclosure procedures


Trustee’s Sale
  • Definition: The sale conducted under a deed of trust after default and foreclosure proceedings
  • Significance: U.S. Bank purchased Aceves’s home at the trustee’s sale on January 9, 2009
  • Distinction: The appellate court allowed the promissory-estoppel and fraud claims to proceed but held that promissory estoppel did not itself provide a basis for voiding the completed sale in the circumstances alleged
