  • [the opinion as excerpted]: Supreme Court of Oregon reviewed and affirmed the judgment for defendant
  • Issue: Whether the jury instructions misapplied the statutory negligence per se doctrine and excused violation principles by allowing reasonableness to negate statutory negligence per se
  • Holding: The Oregon Supreme Court held the instruction was not erroneous in substance because jury could find defendant acted as a reasonably prudent person even if proceeding over the dividing line
  • Rule: Barnum v. Williams, 264 Or. 71 (1972), violation of a motor vehicle statute is negligence as a matter of law unless the violating party introduces evidence from which trier of fact could find the party acted reasonably under the circumstances

  • Reasoning:
  • The court acknowledged a tension between negligence per se and fault-based tort tradition
  • It reviewed its prior doctrine and treated earlier decisions as recognizing emergency or reasonableness as a basis for avoiding per se harshness
  • It rejected illogical confinement of excusal solely to emergency because courts would be tempted to circumvent and because standard remains reasonable care under the circumstances
  • The majority stated present law: if in violation of a motor vehicle statute, negligent as a matter of law unless actor introduces evidence from which trier of fact could find reasonable prudence
  • If no evidence or insufficient evidence, court must find negligence as a matter of law, but if evidence creates fact question, negligence goes to jury
  • It held that because the jury could find defendant acted reasonably, the instruction was not erroneous in substance
  • The dissenting justice argued the exception should be limited to sudden emergency and not merely reasonableness without emergency, but the majority did not adopt that tighter rule
  • Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Plaintiff argued trial court gave erroneous instructions that misapplied statutory negligence per se and allowed excusal without required emergency conditions
  • Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: Defendant argued the instruction correctly reflected present state of law that statutory violation creates presumption of negligence rebuttable by evidence of reasonable conduct
  • Disposition: Supreme Court of Oregon affirmed
  • Importance: Refines how to handle statutory negligence per se in motor vehicle contexts by requiring evidence of reasonableness to avoid negligence as matter of law, even beyond emergency-only framing

----- Case Narrative: Perry v. S.N. (mandatory reporting statute for child abuse, alleged failure to report and subsequent abuse)

Two children, B.N. and K.N., attended a day care center operated by Francis Keller and her husband Daniel Keller from March 25, 1991 to August 28, 1991. The parents of the children, S.N. and S.N., alleged that Daniel Keller regularly abused the children during the time they attended, both physically and sexually. They further alleged that at least on one occasion in August 1991, when visiting the Kellers, three adults (Douglas Perry, Janise White, and Raul Quintero) saw Daniel Keller bring a number of children out into the adjoining home and sexually abuse them. The parents alleged that despite witnessing abuse, these three individuals did not attempt to stop the abuse or report the crimes to police or child welfare officials. They framed this as negligence per se because Texas Family Code provisions required any person who has cause to believe a child’s physical or mental health or welfare has been or may be adversely affected by abuse to report the abuse to state authorities. They also alleged gross negligence and common-law negligence. The legal dispute thus came from the parents’ claim that the day care remained open and enabled ongoing abuse because Perry, White, and Quintero knowingly failed to report suspected child abuse as mandated by statute. The core factual controversy is not about whether reporting was possible if they knew, but about the statutory basis for civil duty and whether negligence per se should be recognized based on criminal reporting provisions when plaintiffs’ injuries occur through third-party wrongdoing

Case Name: Perry v. S.N., 973 S.W.2d 301 (Tex. 1998), Phillips, Chief Justice
  • Document: 206-277
  • Course: Torts, Week 4 — Negligence (Breach)

  • Facts
  • B.N. and K.N. attended a day care center operated by Francis Keller and Daniel Keller from March 25, 1991 to August 28, 1991
  • Parents S.N. and S.N. alleged Daniel Keller regularly abused B.N. and K.N. and other children physically and sexually during the attendance period
  • The parents alleged that at an unspecified time Francis Keller confided in Janise White about Daniel Keller’s “abusive habits toward children”
  • The record alleged that in August 1991, while visiting the Kellers, Douglas Perry, Janise White, and Raul Quintero saw Daniel Keller bring a number of children out of the day care center into the adjoining home and sexually abuse them
  • The record does not indicate whether B.N. and K.N. were among these children
  • Parents alleged Perry, White, and Quintero failed to stop the abuse and knowingly failed to report it to police or child welfare officials
  • Plaintiffs sued individually and as next friends of their children
  • Plaintiffs sought damages including pain, mental anguish, medical expenses, and loss of income
  • Procedural Posture
  • [the opinion as excerpted]: Trial court granted summary judgment for Perry, White, and Quintero and severed their claims from claims against the Kellers
  • Intermediate appellate court (Austin) reversed the summary judgment as to negligence per se and gross negligence and remanded for trial
  • Texas Supreme Court reversed and rendered judgment that plaintiffs take nothing
  • Issue: Whether plaintiffs may maintain a negligence per se cause of action based on the Family Code mandatory child abuse reporting statute requiring knowing failure to report to be a misdemeanor
  • Holding: The Texas Supreme Court held it is not appropriate to adopt the statute as establishing duty and standard of conduct in tort, and thus plaintiffs may not maintain negligence per se or gross negligence based on the defendants’ violation of the child abuse reporting statute
  • Rule: Perry v. S.N., 973 S.W.2d 301 (Tex. 1998), courts will not apply negligence per se when the criminal statute does not provide an appropriate basis for civil liability and must consider whether to impose tort liability based on factors including sole-source duty, clear definition/notice, fault, ruinous damages, and directness of injury

  • Reasoning:
  • The court emphasized duty is a prerequisite to tort liability and that criminal duty to obey does not automatically translate into tort duty
  • It held it must look beyond the specific case to the statute’s full reach because it would otherwise create broad tort exposure
  • It listed threshold questions: plaintiff belongs to class protected and injury is type statute designed to prevent, which the court found satisfied
  • It then addressed appropriateness of imposing tort liability and laid out factors guiding the ultimate fairness/workability/wisdom determination:
  • whether statute is sole source of tort duty or merely supplies a standard for existing common-law duty
  • whether statute clearly defines required conduct
  • whether negligence per se would impose liability without fault (here, statute includes knowing failure)
  • whether negligence per se would impose ruinous damages disproportionate to seriousness of statutory violation, considering broad collateral wrongdoer risk
  • whether plaintiff injury is directly or indirectly resulted from the statutory violation, invoking indirectness where injury is caused by third party’s underlying abuse
  • It concluded negligence per se is not appropriate because decision could not be limited to serious misconduct and because of broad potential liability and indirect injury
  • The court explicitly did not decide whether a differently drawn statute or a statute criminalizing only egregious misconduct might be an appropriate basis
  • Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Plaintiffs argued the statute creates negligence per se and that failure to report proximately caused harm by allowing day care to remain open and enabling ongoing abuse
  • Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: Defendants argued plaintiffs failed to state a cognizable claim because negligence per se based on the criminal reporting statute is not appropriate as a basis for tort duty and standard
  • Disposition: Texas Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals and rendered judgment that plaintiffs take nothing
  • Importance: Shows negligence per se is not automatic even with statutory violation; it emphasizes analyzing appropriateness of imposing tort liability for criminal statute violations with third-party criminal acts and broad indirect injury risks


----- Case Narrative: Dempsey v. Addison Crane Co. (crane rental machine failure and unsafe jib attachment)
A male plaintiff was employed as a pile driver on a construction project in Washington, D.C. in the excavating stage at the corner of 12th and E Streets. The contractor rented a crane from the defendant, a business that rented and operated cranes for others. On March 27, 1962, the crane arrived early in the morning and was moved onto the site excavation. The contractor’s foreman directed the crane operator to move a welding machine that was interfering with progress. The crane operator and assistant proceeded to lift the welding machine and shift it to a new location and then let it down. Four pile drivers, including the injured plaintiff, were holding the welding machine’s corners to prevent twisting. As the welding machine was about to come to rest, an auxiliary jib attached to the boom broke loose, fell, and struck two of the pile drivers holding the corners, killing one and seriously injuring the other who brought this lawsuit. The legal dispute was whether the crane rental company was negligent in two ways, including allegedly leaving the auxiliary jib suspended when not in actual use and allegedly using unsafe means to suspend the jib. The evidence showed the mechanism used involved slings and open hook configurations, and there was also alternative equipment involving shackles that would form a closed loop attachment that was safer. The case thus centered on whether prevailing industry practice to use the open hook slings constituted reasonable care or whether it was unsafe given available safer alternatives

Case Name: Dempsey v. Addison Crane Co., 247 F.Supp. 584 (D.D.C. 1965), Holtzoff, District Judge
  • Document: 206-277
  • Course: Torts, Week 4 — Negligence (Breach)

  • Facts
  • Male plaintiff was a pile driver employed on a construction project at 12th and E Streets in the Northwest section of Washington, D.C
  • On March 27, 1962, his employer rented a crane from defendant Addison Crane Co., which rented and operated cranes
  • Crane arrived early in the morning and was moved on site excavation
  • Contractor’s foreman directed crane operator to move a welding machine interfering with progress
  • Crane operator and assistant lifted the welding machine by crane, shift it, and let it down in new location
  • Four pile drivers, including plaintiff, held the machine corners to prevent twisting
  • As welding machine was about to come to rest, an auxiliary jib attached to the boom broke loose, fell, and hit two pile drivers
  • One pile driver was killed and the other was seriously injured and was the plaintiff
  • Plaintiffs claimed negligence in:
  • leaving the auxiliary jib suspended from the boom when not in actual use
  • unsafe means of suspending the jib
  • The boom was about 60 feet and auxiliary jib about 30 feet
  • Two slings attached jib via metal framework apertures, with open hooks on sling cable ends
  • One hook slipped, increasing load on lower sling, causing lower sling to break and jib to fall
  • Alternative safer apparatus existed using shackles forming closed loop instead of open hook ends
  • Evidence showed apparatus employed was prevailing in the industry at time, though alternative safer equipment existed and was used to lesser extent
  • Slings were not standard equipment and were fabricated by defendant in its shop
  • Procedural Posture
  • U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia: Case tried without a jury, with the court separating liability from damages
  • U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia: The court found defendant liable on the unsafe apparatus charge and resumed damages trial later as described
  • Issue: Whether defendant was negligent in leaving the jib suspended and whether the attachment/suspension method for the auxiliary jib was unsafe and caused the accident, with custom evidence relevant to negligence
  • Holding: The court found no negligence in failure to detach and remove the jib at that moment, but found negligence in the unsafe jib suspension apparatus because it was unsafe as of the date of the accident and was the cause of injury

  • Rule: Dempsey v. Addison Crane Co., 247 F.Supp. 584, 260 (D.D.C. 1965), custom is admissible but not conclusive; what ought to be done is fixed by reasonable prudence not merely by prevailing practice
  • Reasoning:
  • The court analyzed the two negligence charges separately
  • On leaving jib suspended, it concluded plaintiffs did not sustain by fair preponderance of evidence that failure to detach/removal was negligence merely because not in actual use at that moment
  • On unsafe apparatus charge, the court reviewed the jib attachment mechanism in detail
  • It addressed prevailing custom: the apparatus used was widely used in industry and some large concerns used it
  • It acknowledged admissibility of prevailing custom but stated conformity or nonconformity is not conclusive proof of due care
  • It cited the idea that a whole calling may lag in adoption of new devices, and “reasonable prudence is not common prudence” as strict measure
  • It concluded the means and apparatus by which jib attached were unsafe as of the accident date and constituted negligence, and that this negligence caused the injuries
  • Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Defendant was negligent for leaving jib suspended when not in use and for using unsafe attachment means; prevailing use did not excuse unsafe design
  • Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: Defendant argued it used standard prevailing equipment practices in the crane rental industry and thus did not breach due care
  • Disposition: District court found defendant liable on unsafe apparatus negligence and set damages to be tried later
  • Importance: Provides explicit doctrinal treatment of custom evidence, especially rejecting custom as conclusive and using reasonable prudence rather than industry practice as measure of negligence

----- Case Narrative: Shilkret v. Annapolis Emergency Hospital Association (infant brain damage, malpractice standard for physicians and hospitals)

An infant plaintiff, Mark Alan Shilkret, was born at Anne Arundel General Hospital on December 22, 1968 and remained continuously institutionalized due to brain damage allegedly caused by intracranial bleeding at delivery. His parents sued physicians and the hospital for negligence, alleging both delivery and subsequent treatment failures. The case involved multiple doctors: two obstetricians who treated the mother during prenatal stage and delivered the infant, an anesthesiologist at birth, and a pediatrician who allegedly examined the infant the day after birth. The hospital was also named. At trial, the court ruled that the applicable medical malpractice standard was the “strict locality” rule, requiring plaintiffs to prove that the defendants failed to meet the standard of care exercised by physicians in their own community or locality. Because plaintiffs conceded they could not prove under the strict locality rule, they requested leave to make a proffer of expert medical testimony that could meet any other standard and then attempted to proceed with proffered expert testimony in support of a broader standard. The proffered testimony described national standards: one expert, an obstetrician-gynecologist involved with an Army hospital and accredited-hospital affiliations, believed accredited hospitals met national standards in caring for obstetrical patients. Another neurosurgeon expert indicated national standards for neurological diagnosis and treatment and that the defendants violated national standards applicable to child delivery, infant care, and treatment of neurological problems. The central dispute thus became what standard of care should govern medical malpractice in Maryland, and whether plaintiffs could rely on national standards rather than strict locality

Case Name: Shilkret v. Annapolis Emergency Hospital Association, 276 Md. 187 (1975), Levine, Judge
  • Document: 206-277
  • Course: Torts, Week 4 — Negligence (Breach)

  • Facts
  • Infant Mark Alan Shilkret born at Anne Arundel General Hospital on December 22, 1968
  • Infant has been continuously institutionalized since birth due to brain damage alleged to result from intracranial bleeding caused by negligence at delivery
  • Subsequent treatment by defendant physicians and hospital is alleged to have also contributed to the injury
  • Defendants include:
  • two obstetricians who treated mother prenatally and delivered infant
  • an anesthesiologist attending at birth
  • a pediatrician examining infant the day after birth
  • the hospital Anne Arundel General Hospital
  • Trial court ruled strict locality rule applies and directed verdict for defendants because plaintiffs could not meet that standard
  • Plaintiffs conceded inability to prove strict locality and made extensive proffers of experts to meet other standards
  • Obstetrician expert testified about American Hospital Association membership, Joint Commission on Accreditation standards, national standard compliance for accredited hospitals, and his role in Army hospital
  • Neurosurgeon expert testified about national standards for neurological diagnosis and treatment and that defendants violated those national standards
  • The appellate history affirmed directed verdict based on strict locality rule
  • Procedural Posture
  • [the opinion as excerpted]: Trial court directed verdict for defendants under strict locality rule
  • Court of Special Appeals affirmed
  • Court of Appeals of Maryland reversed and remanded for new trial
  • Issue: What standard of care applies in medical malpractice cases in Maryland, including whether the strict locality rule should govern physicians and hospitals or whether a national or similar locality standard should apply
  • Holding: Court of Appeals of Maryland rejected strict locality and held that physicians and hospitals are held to a standard of a reasonably competent practitioner/hospital in same class under same or similar circumstances, taking account of advances and availability of facilities, and held proffered evidence sufficient to take standard-of-care issue to jury
  • Rule: Shilkret v. Annapolis Emergency Hospital Association, 349 A.2d 245 (Md. 1975), duty is degree of care and skill expected of reasonably competent practitioner in same class under same or similar circumstances, and locality rules no longer fit modern medicine

  • Reasoning:
  • The court explained that general negligence principles govern malpractice claims and plaintiffs bear burden to show lack of requisite skill or care
  • It emphasized specialty and specialized knowledge require a standard beyond the ordinary reasonably prudent lay person, but the standard must be fair to both patient and physician
  • It traced history of locality rules and criticized strict locality as too narrow given modern communications, availability of medical literature, training standardization, and changed medical realities
  • It discussed strict locality and similar locality rules as previously developed to protect rural practitioners, but held those rationales no longer fit
  • It explained that specialization and certification have established uniform requirements not governed by geography
  • It held strict locality can no longer be sustained given current state of medical science
  • It also addressed hospitals and found no prior distinction in Maryland and that accreditation and regulation impose statewide standards consistent with reasonable competent standard
  • It held that evidence of national standards for accredited hospitals and specialists and general practitioners was sufficient to send standard-of-care issue to jury as to all appellees
  • It limited the review to standard of care and did not reach whether breach and causation were proven
  • Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Plaintiffs argued strict locality rule should not apply, and proffered national standards through expert testimony
  • Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: Defendants argued strict locality rule controls and plaintiffs failed to meet evidentiary requirements under that rule
  • Disposition: Court of Appeals of Maryland reversed directed verdict and remanded for new trial consistent with its standard-of-care holdings
  • Importance: Updates the negligence “reasonable care” analysis for medical malpractice by rejecting strict locality and adopting a reasonably competent practitioner/hospital standard incorporating national advances and facilities

----- Case Narrative: Helling v. Carey (glaucoma undetected in under-40 patient—profession standard no routine pressure tests)

Barbara Helling, the plaintiff, had primary open angle glaucoma. Glaucoma is described as a condition where nourishing fluids do not flow out of the eye easily, gradually raising pressure and damaging the optic nerve fibers, with first loss usually occurring in the periphery and often few symptoms such that it is undetected until damage becomes extensive and irreversible without a pressure test. The defendants were ophthalmologists Dr. Thomas F. Carey and Dr. Robert C. Laughlin, partners practicing ophthalmology. Helling first consulted the defendants in 1959 for myopia and was fitted with contact lenses. She next consulted in September 1963 concerning irritation from the contact lenses. There were additional consultations in October 1963, February 1967, September 1967, October 1967, May 1968, July 1968, August 1968, September 1968, and October 1968. Until the October 1968 consultation, the defendants considered her visual problems related solely to contact lens complications. On that October 1968 consultation, Dr. Carey tested eye pressure and field of vision for the first time and indicated that Helling had glaucoma. At the time, Helling was thirty-two years old and essentially had lost peripheral vision, with central vision reduced to approximately 5 degrees vertical by 10 degrees horizontal. Thereafter, in August 1969 after consulting other physicians, she filed a complaint alleging the severe and permanent damage resulted proximately from defendants’ negligence. Experts testified that professional standards for ophthalmology in similar circumstances did not require routine pressure tests for glaucoma patients under 40, because the disease rarely occurs in that age group. But the record also established that pressure tests are required when complaints and symptoms reveal glaucoma should be suspected. The dispute became whether, despite professional standards not requiring routine testing under-40 absent suspected signs, reasonable prudence required earlier testing in this unique case where a simple harmless pressure test could have detected glaucoma and potentially avoided grave irreversible vision loss

Case Name: Helling v. Carey, 83 Wn.2d 514 (1974), Hunter, Associate Justice
  • Document: 206-277
  • Course: Torts, Week 4 — Negligence (Breach)

  • Facts
  • Plaintiff Barbara Helling suffered from primary open angle glaucoma
  • Glaucoma causes interference with drainage of nourishing fluids, gradually raising eye pressure
  • Resulting pressure damages optic nerve fibers, causing field loss that begins peripherally
  • Disease often has few symptoms and is often undetected until extensive irreversible damage absent pressure test
  • Defendants were ophthalmologists Dr. Thomas F. Carey and Dr. Robert C. Laughlin, partners practicing ophthalmology
  • Helling first consulted defendants in 1959 for myopia; fitted with contact lenses
  • Consultations: September 1963 (irritation), October 1963, February 1967, September 1967, October 1967, May 1968, July 1968, August 1968, September 1968, and October 1968
  • Until October 1968, defendants attributed visual problems solely to complications associated with contact lenses
  • October 1968: for first time Dr. Carey tested eye pressure and field of vision
  • Results indicated glaucoma had developed; Helling was age 32 at diagnosis
  • By then she had essentially lost peripheral vision and central vision reduced to approximately 5 degrees vertical by 10 degrees horizontal
  • August 1969: Helling filed a complaint against the defendants alleging severe permanent damage proximately resulted from negligence
  • Experts testified standards of ophthalmology do not require routine pressure tests for glaucoma patients under 40, but require tests if complaints and symptoms reveal glaucoma should be suspected
  • Dr. Carey testified incidence of glaucoma under 40 is less than 100 to one per cent (described as about one in 25,000 or less), while over-40 incidence is 2–3 per cent
  • Testimony emphasized that a pressure test is simple, relatively inexpensive, has no judgment factor, results are definitive, and giving it is harmless if eye condition permits
  • The record indicated absence of evidence that the test could not have been timely given
  • Procedural Posture
  • [the opinion as excerpted]: Trial court entered judgment for defendants after defense verdict
  • Court of Appeals affirmed
  • Washington Supreme Court granted review and reversed trial judgment and remanded for damages only
  • Issue: Whether adherence to professional medical standards that do not require routine pressure tests for under-40 patients insulates ophthalmologists from negligence liability in the unique factual circumstances where earlier testing could have prevented grave irreversible harm

  • Holding: Washington Supreme Court held as a matter of law that reasonable prudence required timely pressure testing, defendants were negligent, and remanded for a new trial on damages only
  • Rule: Helling v. Carey, 83 Wn.2d 514 (1974), where a simple, harmless, definitive test would detect glaucoma in time to arrest irreversible harm, reasonable prudence requires timely testing even if the profession’s routine-standard does not require it for under-40 patients
  • Reasoning:
  • The court described the case as unique and found undisputed expert testimony about professional standards
  • It framed the issue as whether compliance with professional standard should insulate from liability where substantial vision was lost due to failure to give timely pressure test
  • It reasoned that one under-40 patient’s entitlement to the same protection as those over 40 requires timely detection for irreversible damage avoidance
  • It invoked Holmes’s and Hand’s formulation about what usually is done is evidence, but what ought to be done is fixed by reasonable prudence and courts must say what is required even if universal disregard by calling would not excuse omission for imperative precautions
  • It held reasonable prudence required timely giving of the simple harmless test, and finding negligence as matter of law was appropriate because there were no disputed facts on liability
  • It tied negligence to proximate result of blindness
  • Plaintiff's/Appellee's Arguments: Plaintiff argued defendants should have provided pressure testing earlier to protect her from glaucoma damage and that expert standards as applied were inadequate under her unique facts
  • Defendant/Appellant's Arguments: Defendants argued adherence to professional standards for under-40 should insulate liability because routine testing is not required where incidence is low
  • Disposition: Washington Supreme Court reversed trial judgment and remanded for a new trial on damages only
  • Importance: Establishes how negligence analysis can override professional custom in a narrow, “unique case” where the precaution is imperative and simple and the harm is severe and irreversible

Residence is not synonymous with citizenship (Robinette v Emmons *2)
A person can reside in one state and be domiciled in another. Miss. Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989)
Two requirements are required to acquire a new domicile, physical presence in the new state and either intention to make a home there indefinitely or the absence of an intention to make a home elsewhere. See Gilbert v. David, 235 U.S. 561, 569-70, 35 S.Ct. 164, 59 L.Ed. 360 (1915)
“A person's previous domicile is not lost until a new one is acquired”. Von Dunser v. Aronoff, 915 F.2d 1071, 1072 (6th Cir.1990)  
“Federal jurisdiction is tested according to the facts as they exist at the time an action is initiated” Television Reception Corp. v. Dunbar, 426 F.2d 174, 177 (6th Cir.1970). 
“Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction,” and “the burden of establishing” a jurisdictional basis “rests upon the party asserting jurisdiction.” Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 114 S. Ct. 1673, 1675 (1994).

**Deasy v. Louisville & Jefferson County Metropolitan Sewer District**
Posture
Plaintiff sued 35 Kentucky defendants under §§ 1331 and 1332
Rule 12(b)(1) granted for lack of subject matter jurisdiction 
Sixth circuit affirmed
Jurisdiction
Deasy wanted to prove that he was a resident of Tennessee, he wanted the court to be in the Western District of Kentucky, they had 1332 jurisdiction over the sewer district claims
The defendants wanted to prove that Deasy was a Kentucky resident, meaning that he and every defendant shared a state, complete diversity would fail and the court would not have subject matter jurisdiction
Facts
Deasy claimed residence in Portland, Tennessee but listed a Louisville, Kentucky address for mail and business
His claimed Tennessee residence was half of his sister’s duplex 
He owned the home he lived in when in Kentucky
He changed his voter registration to Tennessee but never voted there and voted regularly in Kentucky before the change
He was physically present in Tennessee only on weekends 
His daughter had never attended school in Tennessee
Issue
Was Deasy a resident of Tennessee or Kentucky?
Holding
Kentucky was Deasy’s domicile, diversity jurisdiction was lacking 
Reasoning
Deasy presented no evidence inconsistent with a Kentucky domicile
A voter registration change without actual voting did not move the needle
Deasy owned a home in Kentucky while only claiming half of a duplex in Tennessee
Deasy rents his Tennessee home he inhered instead of living there
Relation to Fox Case
Deasy had Kentucky home ownership with presence in Tennessee
Deasy’s primary location was in Kentucky, Fox’s primary location was in Tennessee

**Pitt Excavating, LLC v. Pitt**
Posture
A Tennessee LLC sued its sole member’s ex-wife who was a Kentucky citizen for conversion and breach of fiduciary duty in the US District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee
The district court first found diversity was established
On reconsideration and an evidentiary hearing, this was dismissed for lack of jurisdictional
$22,376.42 were imposed in fees 
Facts 
Mr. Pitt lived at the Kentucky farm awarded to his ex wife in their divorce
He leased an apartment in Madison, Tennessee beginning in November 2012, held a Tennessee CDL and contractor’s license, and paid federal taxes on Tennessee earned income
His ex wife filed an eviction petition in July 2013 leading Pitt to stay exclusively at the Tennessee apartment
He never changed his voter registration from Kentucky and voted in Kentucky in 2012
In a July 2013 filing objecting to the eviction, he stated he had continued to live on the Kentucky estate since 2008
After filing his lawsuit, he signed a materialman’s lien affidavit listing the Kentucky farm as his address
He petitioned a Kentucky court to set aside the divorce decree so as to reclaim the farm
Issue
Whether Mr. Pitt had abandoned his Kentucky domicile and acquired a Tennessee domicile as of the September 10, 2013 filing date
Holding
No, Mr. Pitt remained a Kentucky citizen, diversity was absent and the case was dismissed
Reasoning
Physical presence in Tennessee was satisfied but intent as a Tennessee citizen was not
Presence that is compelled does not move domicile, “one who is in a place solely by virtue of superior force exerted by another should not be held to have abandoned his former domicile.” Stifel, 477 F.2d at 1121; see also Denlinger v. Brennan, 87 F.3d 214, 216 (7th Cir.1996)
Pitt spent two to three nights per week at the Kentucky farm which indicates that he had a continued desire to remain domiciled there
Pitt pursued actions to reclaim his old house which indicated continued attachment to Kentucky domicile
The district court found that the LLC was used to manufacture diversity
Relation to Fox Case
Fox spends one to two nights per week in Kentucky and the rest in Tennessee, under the reasoning of Pitt, the majority of nights in the old domicile is evidence of continuity
Nothing about Fox’s Kentucky presence is compelled but it is not exclusive either

**Robinette v. Emmons**
Posture
Defendant removed the case from state court to federal court
The court sua sponte (on its own accord) ordered a show-cause briefing to determine if the case should continue in the jurisdiction it was in
Only State Farm responded 
The court discharged the show cause order and retained the case
State Farm the defendant wanted Emmons to be a Michigan citizen 
The plaintiffs wanted Emmons to be a Kentucky defendant 
Facts
The complaint alleged that the defendant Emmons was a non-resident of Kentucky who resided in Michigan
State Farm’s notice of removal responded to the allegation with a response that Emmons was a domiciliary and citizen of Michigan 
The defendants showed the Facebook profile of Emmons saying she lived in Kentucky and is from Michigan
Proof that Emmons was not registered to vote in Kentucky and had no Kentucky driver’s license
The defendants presented an address history that showed 13 years of Michigan addresses with only 6 months of Kentucky addresses
Issue
Did the removing defendant meet the burden of establishing diversity
Holding
Yes, Emmons was a Michigan citizen, complete diversity existed and the case was retained
Reasoning
The burden is on the removing defendant 
Emmon’s long term domicile indicated she was a resident of Michigan. Courts consistently
reject such short-term, transient abnormalities as citizenship markers. See, e.g., Myrick, 764 F.3d at 664
Absence of voter registration and driver’s license indicates a desire not to acquire citizenship in Kentucky
Relation to Fox Case
Fox’s Facebook says he lives in Kentucky and he changed it when his house was finished, however the Robinette case establishes that it does not prove much because you can live on one state and intend on returning to another
In Robinette the defendant removed the case successfully and it states that the removing defendant carries the burden, meaning that in the Fox case the burden is on the tech company to prove he is not a Tennessee resident
Robinette says citizenship reflects where one plans to live in the long run, Fox told Casco he hopes to settle in Bowling Green after he marries, however that plan is contingent on something that has not happened. Also domicile is fixed as of the day that the suit was filed (July 2026) when Fox lived in Nashville, worked in Nashville ans was not engaged

Timeline

Summer 2026: Furniture brought to house, spends 1-2 nights a week there and holidays

Discussion
<w:t xml:space="preserve">A federal district court may exercise diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1) only where the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000 and the action between citizens of different states. Diversity must be complete, meaning that no plaintiff may be a citizen of the same state as any defendant. Robinette v. Emmons, No. 7:19-CV-2-REW, 2019 WL 13212618, at *1 (E.D. Ky. Jan. 25, 2019). Because the defendant is incorporated and headquartered in Tennessee, complete diversity exists  only if Fox was a citizen of Kentucky when the suit was initiated in July 2026. A court will likely conclude that he was not. Fox established domicile in Tennessee when he purchased an apartment in Nashville that he continues to lease. He maintains an active Tennessee voter registration under which he has voted, a Tennessee driver’s license, a Tennessee vehicle registration, and a Nashville based music career. Fox dies not hold a Kentucky voter registration, driver’s license or vehicle registration. Fox has purchased a house in Bowling Green, Kentucky, however, it cannot be considered a new domicile as he only spends one to two nights per week at that residence. The motion to remand is likely to succeed.

<w:t xml:space="preserve">A. The defendant bears the burden as abandoning his Tennessee domicile and acquired a new <w:t>one in Kentucky

<w:t xml:space="preserve">Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction and the burden of establishing a jurisdictional basis rests upon the party asserting jurisdiction. Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618 at *1 (citing Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 114 S. Ct. 1673, 1675 (1994)). In Robinette, the court required the removing defendant to present affirmative proof of the disputed party’s citizenship in order to retain the case. This case differed from Deasy and Pitt Excavating, in which the plaintiff had invoked § 1332, thus Deasy was required to prove his domicile. Since Fox chose a Tennessee court, he does need to prove his own citizenship. 
</w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b w:val="false"/><w:bCs w:val="false"/><w:i w:val="false"/><w:iCs w:val="false"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">State citizenship for diversity purposes is equated with domicile. Pitt Excavating, LLC v. Pitt, 603 F. Appx 393, 396 (6th Cir. 2015) (citing Von Dunser v. Aronoff, 915 F.2d 1071, 1072 (6th Cir. 1990)). Residence is not synonymous with citizenship. Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618, at *1 (citing Kaiser v. Loomis, 391 F.2d 1007, 1009 (6th Cir. 1968)). Meaning a person can reside in one state while being domiciled in another. To establish domicile within a particular state, a person must be physically present in the state and must have either the intention to make his home there indefinitely or the absence of intention to make his home elsewhere. Pitt Excavating,, 603 F. Appx 393 (citing Stifel v Hopkins, 477 F.2d 1116, 1120 (6th Cir. 1973)). 
<w:t xml:space="preserve">Fox’s Tennessee domicile is not contestable. He moved to Tennessee in 2019 to attend the University of Tennessee, he then relocated to Nashville after graduating in 2023. He leased an apartment in Nashville, obtained a Tennessee driver’s license, registered his vehicle in Tennessee, and registered to vote in Davidson county. Under Von Dunser, Fox’s Tennessee domicile continues unless the defendant proves a Kentucky domicile replaced it. 

</w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b w:val="false"/><w:bCs w:val="false"/><w:i w:val="false"/><w:iCs w:val="false"/></w:rPr><w:t>B. Fox’s physical presence remains predominantly in Tennessee and the Sixth Circuit has<w:t>treated presence at the original domicile as evidence of a party’s continued domicile there

</w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b w:val="false"/><w:bCs w:val="false"/><w:i w:val="false"/><w:iCs w:val="false"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Pitt Excavating presents a case where Mr. Pitt sought to prove he was domiciled in Tennessee. Mr. Pitt began to stay at an apartment in Madison, Tennessee in November 2012 but did not begin to stay there exclusively until after eviction proceedings began in July 2013. However the court found Pitt’s behavior was “highly probative of a continuing desire to remain domiciled at the Kentucky farm” because he would still spend two to three nights per week at the farm up until September 2013. The court concluded that spending four to five nights per week in Tennessee in the weeks leading up to the case not sufficient to demonstrate that he abandoned his Kentucky domicile. 
<w:t xml:space="preserve">Fox’s claim is stronger than Mr. Pitt, he spends only one to two nights a week in Bowling Green and the remaining five or six days in Nashville. If residing two to three nights per week in the original domicile in the Pitt case was evidence of a continued domicile in Kentucky then Fox spending most nights in Tennessee would be strong evidence of Tennessee domicile. 
<w:t xml:space="preserve">Deasy reinforces this point because the plaintiff claimed Tennessee domicile but he was physically present in Tennessee only on weekends while the home he owned was in Kentucky, 47 F. Appx 728. Ultimately the court determined that Deasy was a Kentucky domiciliary. The pattern of living for Fox is the opposite, he spends weekdays in Nashville and the weekends and holidays in Bowling Green. 

<w:t xml:space="preserve">C. The defendant’s evidence establishes a second residence, not a change of domiciled

<w:t xml:space="preserve">The defendant’s argument that Fox is a Kentucky resident relies on Fox’s ownership of his Bowling Green property, however, ownership of property is not domicile. In Deasy, the plaintiff owned a house and a duplex in Tennessee, however this fact was not sufficient to establish Tennessee domicile because he rented the house to someone else and trips to Tennessee were infrequent. 47 F. Appx 728. In Pitt Excavating, Mr. Pitt was determined to be a Kentucky resident even though he did not even own the property on which he resided. Pitt Excavating, 603 F. Appx 394-97. These cases both apply  the principle established in Stifel which is that proving citizenship requires showing domicile not just residence. Fox uses the Bowling Green residence only on the weekends and holidays, it only furnished minimally and has only been connected to utilities for a few months. This does not reflect a house that is being occupied as a primary residence.
<w:t xml:space="preserve">Since Fox’s residence in Kentucky has been brief, this strengthens his argument as a Tennessee citizen. Courts “consistently reject short-term, transient abnormalities as citizenship markers.” Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618, at *2. In Robinette, the plaintiff’s six month address in Kentucky did not override a thirteen year pattern of residence in Michigan. Fox’s Kentucky house has been finished for only six months, while he has a pattern of residence in Tennessee since 2019.
</w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b w:val="false"/><w:bCs w:val="false"/><w:i w:val="false"/><w:iCs w:val="false"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Fox changed his Facebook profile to say that he lives in Kentucky when the house there was completed. This is addressed by Robinette, where the court considered a print-out of Emmon’s Facebook profile saying that she currently lives in Kentucky and is from Michigan, this however, was not strong enough evidence to indicate that Emmons was a Kentucky citizen. Thus Fox’s social media profile is not sufficient to establish him as a Kentucky resident especially when other factors such as voter registration, vehicle registration and living patterns point to his status as a Tennessee citizen. 
<w:t xml:space="preserve">The promotional flyer for one of Fox’s shows is not sufficient evidence of Kentucky citizenship either. Fox holds that he did not create nor approve it the flyer which is credited to CSP Marketing. Stifel establishes that intent to domicile in a different state can be expressed through actions the party undertakes himself such as affidavits, registrations, opening bank accounts, etc. Since the flyer was created by a third party, this is weak evidence. 

<w:t xml:space="preserve">D. Fox’s deisre to settle in Bowling Green after marrying is contingent on future plans which <w:t>have not occurred yet and do not effect a change of domicile

<w:t xml:space="preserve">The defendant’s strongest argument is that Fox hopes to settle in Bowling Green when he marries his girlfriend. Citizenship reflects a person’s long term plan for state of habitation rather than just current residence. Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618, at *2 (citing Myrick v. Wellpoint, Inc., 764 F.3d 662, 664 (7th Cir. 2014)). The defendant will argue that this is evidence that Fox intends for his long term residence to be Kentucky. 
<w:t xml:space="preserve">This argument fails because domicile is fixed by the facts as they existed when the suit was initiated. Pitt Excavating, 603 F. Appx 396 (citing Dunbar, 426 F.2d 174, 177 (6th Cir. 1970)). As of July 2026, Fox had not proposed, was not engaged, and was not married. An intention to relocate to another state at an unspecified time in the future is not an intention to establish domicile nor does it indicate the absence of an intention to make a home elsewhere. 
</w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b w:val="false"/><w:bCs w:val="false"/><w:i w:val="false"/><w:iCs w:val="false"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Fox did not indicate that he intended to abandon Tennessee citizenship because he said he plans to live in Nashville for at least the next few years because Nashville is where his regular gigs are played and where his income comes from. He added that even after any potential move to Kentucky, he would still commute to Nashville for work. Because Fox expects to continue earning income in Tennessee indefinitely and states that he will continue living there for the coming years, he has not formed a present intention to make Kentucky his home indefinitely. 

<w:t>E. Conclusion

<w:t xml:space="preserve">The defendant cannot carry the burden of proving that Fox is a Kentucky citizen. Fox’s physical presence is predominately in Tennessee and exceeds the presence that Pitt had at his original domicile in Kentucky in Pitt Excavating. The objective signs of intent that the Sixth Circuit relied on in Deasy and Pitt Excavating point to Tennessee in Fox’s case. Deasy found insufficient evidence inconsistent with a Kentucky domicile. 47 F. Appx 728. Fox presents stronger evidence indicating evidence against a Kentucky domicile he has a Nashville lease, an active Tennessee voter registration, a Tennessee license, a Tennessee vehicle registration, and a music career based in Nashville. The defendant’s case for Fox being a Kentucky citizen rests upon his recently finished Bowling Green house, his social media profile, and a promoter’s flyer advertising his show. A court will likely find that Fox remains a citizen of Tennessee when the suit was initiated and that complete diversity is absent.

Residence is not synonymous with citizenship (Robinette v Emmons *2)
A person can reside in one state and be domiciled in another. Miss. Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989)
Two requirements are required to acquire a new domicile, physical presence in the new state and either intention to make a home there indefinitely or the absence of an intention to make a home elsewhere. See Gilbert v. David, 235 U.S. 561, 569-70, 35 S.Ct. 164, 59 L.Ed. 360 (1915)
“A person's previous domicile is not lost until a new one is acquired”. Von Dunser v. Aronoff, 915 F.2d 1071, 1072 (6th Cir.1990)
“Federal jurisdiction is tested according to the facts as they exist at the time an action is initiated” Television Reception Corp. v. Dunbar, 426 F.2d 174, 177 (6th Cir.1970).
“Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction,” and “the burden of establishing” a jurisdictional basis “rests upon the party asserting jurisdiction.” Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 114 S. Ct. 1673, 1675 (1994).

Deasy v. Louisville & Jefferson County Metropolitan Sewer District
Posture
Plaintiff sued 35 Kentucky defendants under §§ 1331 and 1332
Rule 12(b)(1) granted for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
Sixth circuit affirmed
Jurisdiction
Deasy wanted to prove that he was a resident of Tennessee, he wanted the court to be in the Western District of Kentucky, they had 1332 jurisdiction over the sewer district claims
The defendants wanted to prove that Deasy was a Kentucky resident, meaning that he and every defendant shared a state, complete diversity would fail and the court would not have subject matter jurisdiction
Facts
Deasy claimed residence in Portland, Tennessee but listed a Louisville, Kentucky address for mail and business
His claimed Tennessee residence was half of his sister’s duplex
He owned the home he lived in when in Kentucky
He changed his voter registration to Tennessee but never voted there and voted regularly in Kentucky before the change
He was physically present in Tennessee only on weekends
His daughter had never attended school in Tennessee
Issue
Was Deasy a resident of Tennessee or Kentucky?
Holding
Kentucky was Deasy’s domicile, diversity jurisdiction was lacking
Reasoning
Deasy presented no evidence inconsistent with a Kentucky domicile
A voter registration change without actual voting did not move the needle
Deasy owned a home in Kentucky while only claiming half of a duplex in Tennessee
Deasy rents his Tennessee home he inhered instead of living there
Relation to Fox Case
Deasy had Kentucky home ownership with presence in Tennessee
Deasy’s primary location was in Kentucky, Fox’s primary location was in Tennessee

Pitt Excavating, LLC v. Pitt
Posture
A Tennessee LLC sued its sole member’s ex-wife who was a Kentucky citizen for conversion and breach of fiduciary duty in the US District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee
The district court first found diversity was established
On reconsideration and an evidentiary hearing, this was dismissed for lack of jurisdictional
$22,376.42 were imposed in fees
Facts
Mr. Pitt lived at the Kentucky farm awarded to his ex wife in their divorce
He leased an apartment in Madison, Tennessee beginning in November 2012, held a Tennessee CDL and contractor’s license, and paid federal taxes on Tennessee earned income
His ex wife filed an eviction petition in July 2013 leading Pitt to stay exclusively at the Tennessee apartment
He never changed his voter registration from Kentucky and voted in Kentucky in 2012
In a July 2013 filing objecting to the eviction, he stated he had continued to live on the Kentucky estate since 2008
After filing his lawsuit, he signed a materialman’s lien affidavit listing the Kentucky farm as his address
He petitioned a Kentucky court to set aside the divorce decree so as to reclaim the farm
Issue
Whether Mr. Pitt had abandoned his Kentucky domicile and acquired a Tennessee domicile as of the September 10, 2013 filing date
Holding
No, Mr. Pitt remained a Kentucky citizen, diversity was absent and the case was dismissed
Reasoning
Physical presence in Tennessee was satisfied but intent as a Tennessee citizen was not
Presence that is compelled does not move domicile, “one who is in a place solely by virtue of superior force exerted by another should not be held to have abandoned his former domicile.” Stifel, 477 F.2d at 1121; see also Denlinger v. Brennan, 87 F.3d 214, 216 (7th Cir.1996)
Pitt spent two to three nights per week at the Kentucky farm which indicates that he had a continued desire to remain domiciled there
Pitt pursued actions to reclaim his old house which indicated continued attachment to Kentucky domicile
The district court found that the LLC was used to manufacture diversity
Relation to Fox Case
Fox spends one to two nights per week in Kentucky and the rest in Tennessee, under the reasoning of Pitt, the majority of nights in the old domicile is evidence of continuity
Nothing about Fox’s Kentucky presence is compelled but it is not exclusive either

Robinette v. Emmons
Posture
Defendant removed the case from state court to federal court
The court sua sponte (on its own accord) ordered a show-cause briefing to determine if the case should continue in the jurisdiction it was in
Only State Farm responded
The court discharged the show cause order and retained the case
State Farm the defendant wanted Emmons to be a Michigan citizen
The plaintiffs wanted Emmons to be a Kentucky defendant
Facts
The complaint alleged that the defendant Emmons was a non-resident of Kentucky who resided in Michigan
State Farm’s notice of removal responded to the allegation with a response that Emmons was a domiciliary and citizen of Michigan
The defendants showed the Facebook profile of Emmons saying she lived in Kentucky and is from Michigan
Proof that Emmons was not registered to vote in Kentucky and had no Kentucky driver’s license
The defendants presented an address history that showed 13 years of Michigan addresses with only 6 months of Kentucky addresses
Issue
Did the removing defendant meet the burden of establishing diversity
Holding
Yes, Emmons was a Michigan citizen, complete diversity existed and the case was retained
Reasoning
The burden is on the removing defendant
Emmon’s long term domicile indicated she was a resident of Michigan. Courts consistently
reject such short-term, transient abnormalities as citizenship markers. See, e.g., Myrick, 764 F.3d at 664
Absence of voter registration and driver’s license indicates a desire not to acquire citizenship in Kentucky
Relation to Fox Case
Fox’s Facebook says he lives in Kentucky and he changed it when his house was finished, however the Robinette case establishes that it does not prove much because you can live on one state and intend on returning to another
In Robinette the defendant removed the case successfully and it states that the removing defendant carries the burden, meaning that in the Fox case the burden is on the tech company to prove he is not a Tennessee resident
Robinette says citizenship reflects where one plans to live in the long run, Fox told Casco he hopes to settle in Bowling Green after he marries, however that plan is contingent on something that has not happened. Also domicile is fixed as of the day that the suit was filed (July 2026) when Fox lived in Nashville, worked in Nashville ans was not engaged

Why Plaintiff sued

Pitt was a Kentucky citizen
Emmons was a Michigan citizen alone


Timeline
2019: Moves to Knoxville, TN for University
2020: Registers car in Tennessee, changes driver’s license to Tennessee
2023: Graduates, moves to Nashville, leases 118 Shelby Ave
Aug 18, 2023: Registers to vote in Davidson County
2024: Buys land near Bowling Green
August 1 2024: Votes in State Primary
November 5, 2024: Votes in General election
Feb 2026: Bowling Green house completed
March 2026: Starts electric, water, and internet to the KY House
June 5-9, 2026: Music City Pro Audio invoice, billed to Nashville address, shipped to Kentucky address
June 10, 2026: Warren County dog license issued, certified from East Nashville Veterinary clinic
June 19, 2026: Blue Anchor Room show in Nashville, Fox promoted as Kentucky’s ownership
Summer 2026: Furniture brought to house, spends 1-2 nights a week there and holidays
July 2026: Files suit in Davidson County, defendant removes case

Discussion
A federal district court may exercise diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1) only where the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000 and the action between citizens of different states. Diversity must be complete, meaning that no plaintiff may be a citizen of the same state as any defendant. Robinette v. Emmons, No. 7:19-CV-2-REW, 2019 WL 13212618, at *1 (E.D. Ky. Jan. 25, 2019). Because the defendant is incorporated and headquartered in Tennessee, complete diversity exists only if Fox was a citizen of Kentucky when the suit was initiated in July 2026. A court will likely conclude that he was not. Fox established domicile in Tennessee when he purchased an apartment in Nashville that he continues to lease. He maintains an active Tennessee voter registration under which he has voted, a Tennessee driver’s license, a Tennessee vehicle registration, and a Nashville based music career. Fox dies not hold a Kentucky voter registration, driver’s license or vehicle registration. Fox has purchased a house in Bowling Green, Kentucky, however, it cannot be considered a new domicile as he only spends one to two nights per week at that residence. The motion to remand is likely to succeed.

A. The defendant bears the burden as abandoning his Tennessee domicile and acquired a new one in Kentucky

Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction and the burden of establishing a jurisdictional basis rests upon the party asserting jurisdiction. Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618 at *1 (citing Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 114 S. Ct. 1673, 1675 (1994)). In Robinette, the court required the removing defendant to present affirmative proof of the disputed party’s citizenship in order to retain the case. This case differed from Deasy and Pitt Excavating, in which the plaintiff had invoked § 1332, thus Deasy was required to prove his domicile. Since Fox chose a Tennessee court, he does need to prove his own citizenship.
State citizenship for diversity purposes is equated with domicile. Pitt Excavating, LLC v. Pitt, 603 F. Appx 393, 396 (6th Cir. 2015) (citing Von Dunser v. Aronoff, 915 F.2d 1071, 1072 (6th Cir. 1990)). Residence is not synonymous with citizenship. Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618, at *1 (citing Kaiser v. Loomis, 391 F.2d 1007, 1009 (6th Cir. 1968)). Meaning a person can reside in one state while being domiciled in another. To establish domicile within a particular state, a person must be physically present in the state and must have either the intention to make his home there indefinitely or the absence of intention to make his home elsewhere. Pitt Excavating,, 603 F. Appx 393 (citing Stifel v Hopkins, 477 F.2d 1116, 1120 (6th Cir. 1973)).
Fox’s Tennessee domicile is not contestable. He moved to Tennessee in 2019 to attend the University of Tennessee, he then relocated to Nashville after graduating in 2023. He leased an apartment in Nashville, obtained a Tennessee driver’s license, registered his vehicle in Tennessee, and registered to vote in Davidson county. Under Von Dunser, Fox’s Tennessee domicile continues unless the defendant proves a Kentucky domicile replaced it.

B. Fox’s physical presence remains predominantly in Tennessee and the Sixth Circuit hastreated presence at the original domicile as evidence of a party’s continued domicile there

Pitt Excavating presents a case where Mr. Pitt sought to prove he was domiciled in Tennessee. Mr. Pitt began to stay at an apartment in Madison, Tennessee in November 2012 but did not begin to stay there exclusively until after eviction proceedings began in July 2013. However the court found Pitt’s behavior was “highly probative of a continuing desire to remain domiciled at the Kentucky farm” because he would still spend two to three nights per week at the farm up until September 2013. The court concluded that spending four to five nights per week in Tennessee in the weeks leading up to the case not sufficient to demonstrate that he abandoned his Kentucky domicile.
Fox’s claim is stronger than Mr. Pitt, he spends only one to two nights a week in Bowling Green and the remaining five or six days in Nashville. If residing two to three nights per week in the original domicile in the Pitt case was evidence of a continued domicile in Kentucky then Fox spending most nights in Tennessee would be strong evidence of Tennessee domicile.
Deasy reinforces this point because the plaintiff claimed Tennessee domicile but he was physically present in Tennessee only on weekends while the home he owned was in Kentucky, 47 F. Appx 728. Ultimately the court determined that Deasy was a Kentucky domiciliary. The pattern of living for Fox is the opposite, he spends weekdays in Nashville and the weekends and holidays in Bowling Green.

C. The defendant’s evidence establishes a second residence, not a change of domiciled

The defendant’s argument that Fox is a Kentucky resident relies on Fox’s ownership of his Bowling Green property, however, ownership of property is not domicile. In Deasy, the plaintiff owned a house and a duplex in Tennessee, however this fact was not sufficient to establish Tennessee domicile because he rented the house to someone else and trips to Tennessee were infrequent. 47 F. Appx 728. In Pitt Excavating, Mr. Pitt was determined to be a Kentucky resident even though he did not even own the property on which he resided. Pitt Excavating, 603 F. Appx 394-97. These cases both apply the principle established in Stifel which is that proving citizenship requires showing domicile not just residence. Fox uses the Bowling Green residence only on the weekends and holidays, it only furnished minimally and has only been connected to utilities for a few months. This does not reflect a house that is being occupied as a primary residence.
Since Fox’s residence in Kentucky has been brief, this strengthens his argument as a Tennessee citizen. Courts “consistently reject short-term, transient abnormalities as citizenship markers.” Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618, at *2. In Robinette, the plaintiff’s six month address in Kentucky did not override a thirteen year pattern of residence in Michigan. Fox’s Kentucky house has been finished for only six months, while he has a pattern of residence in Tennessee since 2019.
Fox changed his Facebook profile to say that he lives in Kentucky when the house there was completed. This is addressed by Robinette, where the court considered a print-out of Emmon’s Facebook profile saying that she currently lives in Kentucky and is from Michigan, this however, was not strong enough evidence to indicate that Emmons was a Kentucky citizen. Thus Fox’s social media profile is not sufficient to establish him as a Kentucky resident especially when other factors such as voter registration, vehicle registration and living patterns point to his status as a Tennessee citizen.
The promotional flyer for one of Fox’s shows is not sufficient evidence of Kentucky citizenship either. Fox holds that he did not create nor approve it the flyer which is credited to CSP Marketing. Stifel establishes that intent to domicile in a different state can be expressed through actions the party undertakes himself such as affidavits, registrations, opening bank accounts, etc. Since the flyer was created by a third party, this is weak evidence.

D. Fox’s deisre to settle in Bowling Green after marrying is contingent on future plans which have not occurred yet and do not effect a change of domicile

The defendant’s strongest argument is that Fox hopes to settle in Bowling Green when he marries his girlfriend. Citizenship reflects a person’s long term plan for state of habitation rather than just current residence. Robinette, 2019 WL 13212618, at *2 (citing Myrick v. Wellpoint, Inc., 764 F.3d 662, 664 (7th Cir. 2014)). The defendant will argue that this is evidence that Fox intends for his long term residence to be Kentucky.
This argument fails because domicile is fixed by the facts as they existed when the suit was initiated. Pitt Excavating, 603 F. Appx 396 (citing Dunbar, 426 F.2d 174, 177 (6th Cir. 1970)). As of July 2026, Fox had not proposed, was not engaged, and was not married. An intention to relocate to another state at an unspecified time in the future is not an intention to establish domicile nor does it indicate the absence of an intention to make a home elsewhere.
Fox did not indicate that he intended to abandon Tennessee citizenship because he said he plans to live in Nashville for at least the next few years because Nashville is where his regular gigs are played and where his income comes from. He added that even after any potential move to Kentucky, he would still commute to Nashville for work. Because Fox expects to continue earning income in Tennessee indefinitely and states that he will continue living there for the coming years, he has not formed a present intention to make Kentucky his home indefinitely.

E. Conclusion

The defendant cannot carry the burden of proving that Fox is a Kentucky citizen. Fox’s physical presence is predominately in Tennessee and exceeds the presence that Pitt had at his original domicile in Kentucky in Pitt Excavating. The objective signs of intent that the Sixth Circuit relied on in Deasy and Pitt Excavating point to Tennessee in Fox’s case. Deasy found insufficient evidence inconsistent with a Kentucky domicile. 47 F. Appx 728. Fox presents stronger evidence indicating evidence against a Kentucky domicile he has a Nashville lease, an active Tennessee voter registration, a Tennessee license, a Tennessee vehicle registration, and a music career based in Nashville. The defendant’s case for Fox being a Kentucky citizen rests upon his recently finished Bowling Green house, his social media profile, and a promoter’s flyer advertising his show. A court will likely find that Fox remains a citizen of Tennessee when the suit was initiated and that complete diversity is absent.
